[h3] 5/10 [/h3]
A decent game if you get it on a hefty discount, but certainly not worth full price. Honestly just go buy SE4 instead if you want to have a fun time and not feel like you're doing some chores.

## 🎯 Single Player  
The base campaign maps (without DLC) look great – big, detailed, and atmospheric. Some areas are perfect for stealth, but I often wish there were more opportunities for true long-range sniping. The level design is impressive, but replaying missions quickly becomes repetitive.  

For achievement hunters, it can be exhausting. A good example is the “Wolf Mountain” mission with Hitler – killing him in a dozen different ways just to unlock achievements feels like filler content. It adds hours of repetition without much creativity from the developers.  

I’ve logged around 350 hours in the game, and while the campaign is enjoyable, replay fatigue is definitely real.  

---

## ⚔️ Axis Invasion  
Axis Invasion is probably the most exciting addition to Sniper Elite 5. Dropping in as a Jäger sniper to hunt down another player completely changes the atmosphere of the campaign. It’s tense, unpredictable, and often thrilling.  

Unfortunately, this mode suffers from serious balance issues – usually against the invader:  
- You can’t loot fallen soldiers for extra weapons, traps, or grenades. You’re stuck with two grenades, a mine, and a medkit.  
- The invaded player has big advantages: looting gear, using phones to track you, and even seeing hints of where you’re approaching from.  
- Worst of all, “Sniper Focus” feels like an unfair advantage – allowing the invaded player to see your location through walls and prepare an ambush.  

Camping makes it worse. Many players clear the entire map of AI, plant mines everywhere, and then sit in a high spot (like a church tower) with perfect vision. Most of my deaths as an invader were simply from running into yet another mine.  

AI isn’t helpful either. If enemies are shooting at the campaign player, I should get an exact location update. Footstep sounds are also too quiet, making sound-based tracking unreliable.  

---

## 🛡️ Survival  
Survival mode is fun, but it highlights a big flaw across the game: there’s no proper tutorial explaining mechanics, scoring, or what actions give the most points. You have to figure it all out yourself.  

Difficulty scaling is also frustrating. Getting a gold medal feels almost impossible on lower difficulties like *Civilian* or *Very Easy*. Maps are sometimes designed to overwhelm you with enemies from all sides, leaving no chance to respond. The mode is intense, but it lacks balance.  

---

## 🔫 Multiplayer  
I’ve only played a few dozen matches, but the main issue is clear: **everything requires grinding**.  
- You unlock weapon attachments in the campaign, but then you must unlock them again in Axis Invasion.  
- In Survival, you also need unlocks, or you’re stuck with bare-bones gear.  
- In Multiplayer, you have to grind all the way to level 50 to access the full arsenal.  

This system feels unfair – new players are stuck with basic weapons, long aim times, and no attachments, while higher-level players dominate. On top of that, there’s a “Prestige” system where you re-grind levels from scratch for small perks. Honestly, it feels lazy.  

Other issues:  
- **Easy Anti-Cheat** doesn’t seem to stop cheaters, but it does eat resources, cause micro-stutters, and add lag.  
- The **wheel menu** is clunky. In combat, it blocks the screen and wastes time. Hotkeys for ammo and explosives would’ve been better.  
- **Weapon customization** is excellent, but loadouts reset across game modes. And you can’t name custom loadouts, which makes things confusing.  

---

## ✅ Pros  
- Beautiful maps and textures  
- Axis Invasion is exciting and unique  
- Wide choice of sniper rifles and secondary weapons  
- Deep and satisfying weapon customization  

## ❌ Cons  
- Repetitiveness kills replay value  
- Poor balance in Axis Invasion  
- Too much grinding across every mode  
- Easy Anti-Cheat hurts performance  
- Wheel menu slows gameplay  
- Lack of realism in animations, physics, and AI  

---

## 📝 Final Thoughts  
Sniper Elite 5 is a good game – even a very good one in some areas – with beautiful visuals, strong sniping mechanics, and a brilliant idea in Axis Invasion. But it also feels unfinished, with too much grinding, weak AI, and mechanics that often frustrate more than they entertain.  

For me, Sniper Elite 2 / Sniper Elite V2 Remastered still holds the crown for the most satisfying overall experience. Sniper Elite 5 is revolutionary in parts, but disappointing in others.  

My advice? Wait for a good sale, grab the Season Pass bundles, and give it a try. It’s worth playing – just be ready for grind, bugs, and missed opportunities.

This is a good game with plenty of replayability, so long as you're willing to accept a more dated paradigm that limits where you can go on the map.  There are some large areas that you can explore freely, but a significant portion of each map consists of intersecting paths with walls (hedges, buildings, etc.) on either side.  There are plenty of places to explore, multi-story buildings, ladders, and so on to keep the terrain interesting within those boundaries.  Because the maps are so huge and the paths have so many intersections, the limitations aren't really a problem; but people who are accustomed to open world games may be in for a bit of a shock.

The shooting mechanics are excellent.  You can choose to stay in 3rd person for the non-scoped weapons, but if you go into 1st person view (C on the keyboard), you'll find a pretty realistic experience with sight movement, wind, bullet arc, and so on.  The anatomically-correct impact camera is shockingly accurate, both in its depiction of bullet trajectory and the gory details of what happens to targets based on the location of impact.  I find it refreshing for a shooter franchise to accurately simulate the effects of bullets, explosives, and the environment, rather than treating every character and object as a bag of hit points with two or three hit boxes.  An inch in one direction or another actually matters in this game.  Fair warning: it's quite gory.

For the most part, stealth and enemy AI are well done.  Once you understand the idiosyncracies of the game, it's a lot of fun to sneak around and take out enemies.  However, if you don't understand the range at which enemies can hear each of your weapons (which, again, is pretty realistic), how to use the environment to mask the sound of gunshots, or how to avoid getting surrounded, you may be headed for a rough time.  This game does a good job of rewarding skill and punishes tactical mistakes fairly harshly.  My one criticism is that if you alert some enemies, they'll sometimes call in ALL their buddies and camp out in the area of the disturbance for quite a long time.  On one hand, this is somewhat realistic, since they actively investigate the places where you might be, check corpses, and investigate malfunctioning equipment.  However, if you don't understand that this is going to happen, you could end up being mobbed by 20 enemies from all directions who then proceed to hang out around your hiding place for 5 minutes.  Pro tip: if you or your shots are detected, move immediately.  Don't move into an area until you have cleared an escape route from that area.

The map and objectives are also quite interesting.  As you explore and gather intel, you'll uncover more objectives or details about existing objectives.  You'll learn safe combinations (so you don't have to spend explosives to open them), find hidden weapon stashes, and learn about advantageous sniping perches.  This game heavily rewards exploration, and is better for it.

Overall, this is a good game for fans of stealth-heavy shooters.  Just be aware that it doesn't follow some modern trends that you may be accustomed to.

Compared to earlier entries into the franchise, Sniper Elite 5 is a little arcade-y. They've worsened many of the stealth features: there are less noise sources to disguise shots, the level design can be a little close quarters at times, and the AI is generally less predictable in a bad way, as in unrealistic. It seems that stealth isn't always an option anymore, which is a risky design choice seeing as the entire premise of the series is that you're a sniper. 

Although the traversal system aims to turn SE into a more immersive direction, making you more of an action figure who can jump and climb anywhere, the implementation is pretty rough, and there is quite a lot of geometry which breaks the realism, and otherwise frustrates the player. 

I found myself playing SE 5 more naturally, by which I mean the learning curve is quite gentle, but I fear that's because they've simplified things for the masses. Let's face it, most of the player base likes the idea of stealth, but ultimately after one mistake they go guns blazing. It seems Rebellion is leaning into that tendency. This would explain why there seems to be less sniper nests, and generally less emphasis on proper positioning. You can quite easily run away or gun everyone down to get that ALL CLEAR and start again. The same can be said for the weapon customisation. It's simply too easy to get the best guns and even the camo unlocks are ridiculous, as in the contrast and scaling not the historically-accurate design. 

The SE5 graphics seem on par with SE4 but I am getting more screen tearing with the newer release, and there are some lighting issues, particularly with vegetation, which is a big loss for a sniper game. Let's not even get into the story because this is Sniper Elite, and if you're here for fleshed-out dialogues and developed characters, you're playing the wrong game. 

So, who is playing this game, and enjoying it? Well, if you like the idea of walking around in a faux-stealth fashion, whereby you can coincidentally time a sniper shot with a passing plane but most of the time opt for your SMG or pistol, in a historically significant setting that is generally interesting to explore, then this game is a good addition to your casual roster. However, I do fear that the Sniper Elite formula is quickly becoming outdated and there will need to be an entire overhaul, both in terms of graphics and game engine, if the franchise wants to remain relevant for much longer.

In general, I enjoyed the game and did get my money's worth out of it (55.2 hours of gameplay to finish the Campaign, but I'm not going to try for 100% Achievements since there are many I'll never get -- nor will I play the other modes).  But, even though the game was released over 3 years ago, it still has many irritating aspects and bugs.  So, since there are plenty of Recommend reviews, I'm going with a Not Recommended here.  Here are the details of my gripes:
[list]
[*] Every time I start the game, it opens a browser and navigates to https://www.epicgames.com/id/activate?userCode=... trying to get me to link my Steam game to an Epic account.  This has been reported since at least 2022.
[*] Every time I join my wife's game to play the campaign in Co-op, it defaults to the Monika Grep character instead of the Harry Hawker character I always select.
[*] I suppose that there must have been at least one World War II black, female, Scott in Special Ops somewhere.  But, I find it irritating that the developers are emphasizing that character.  If they'd have not made her a Scott (thus widening the pool of possible candidates), I'd have been fine with it.
[*] The secondary missions that appear as we move through the maps seems to be designed to draw out the game (which doesn't need it since each mission takes roughly 6 hours to complete).  Almost invariably, as we move through the maps and discover things that spawn those secondary missions, the actual mission location is somewhere far behind us instead of somewhere in the vicinity or somewhat ahead.
[*] Randomly, the crowbar and bolt cutters disappear from our inventories.  This has been reported since at least 2022.
[*] Once again, the pistols in the game (specifically, the Welrod) are ridiculously underpowered.  I refuse to believe that being shot with any pistol at close range would do less damage than merely throwing the pistol at the enemy instead.  Many a time, the wife and I would pump 4 or 5 pistol shots each into the head of some nearby enemy and have him shrug them off.  It's gotten to the point that I'll just close with the enemy and melee him instead of shooting him with those worthless pistols.
[*] The apparently random ability of our characters to vault over minor obstructions is really annoying.  Sometimes, we can climb walls and jump over small fences.  Other times, we can't.  Pick one.
[*] Destroying tanks is ridiculously hard and persnickety.  What's the point of having flashing red weak areas on tanks, and the existence of panzerfausts, anti-tank guns, mines and armor piercing ammunition if none of them actually kill the tank?
[*] Mission 7's stone eagles (and one in Mission 8) and some other collectibles are crazy hidden.  They're completely un-findable without a walk-through.  Those kinds of collectibles should be discoverable with a standard, thorough exploration of the map.  Not hidden-away and visible from just one spot while looking in a specific direction.
[*] I don't know if this is a function of my wife having played through parts of the game before, but several times, we've run into blue-eyeball sub-objectives on the map that are missing the actual task we're supposed to do.  Specifically, activating alternate starting locations.  In Mission 7, we ran into a safe where we were told we'd found the intel we needed to open it.  But, when we went back to the safe, we still couldn't open it.  When we blew the safe with a satchel charge, there was nothing at all in it.  And, the blue-eyeball icon on the map refused to disappear and kept nagging us about opening the safe and telling us it was a couple of meters away from us no matter which direction we approached it from.
[*] After finishing the campaign, I noticed I had not gotten the Tinkerer Achievement/Medal.  It said I'd interacted with only 23 of 24 workbenches.  Yet, examining the details of each of the 8 missions with workbenches shows that I'd gotten 3 workbenches in each.  Since 8 x 3 = 24 (not 23), and I KNOW that I found and interacted with all 3 workbenches in all 8 missions, that medal appears to be bugged.
[*] After a while, the game seems to stop making Auto Backups.
[*] While playing co-op, the game disconnected us several times.  Also, one time the game crashed my entire computer.  I can't remember the last time I've had a computer crash (it's got to have been multiple decades ago).
[*] And, finally, the game uses Denuvo anti-tamper, kernel level anti-cheat, and Easy Anti-Cheat.
[/list]

A Sharpshooter’s Masterclass in Tactical Gameplay

Sniper Elite 5 hits the mark in nearly every category that matters. It’s a masterfully crafted tactical shooter that combines stunning visuals, immersive realism, and finely tuned gameplay to deliver one of the most satisfying sniper experiences to date.

From the moment you load into your first mission, the graphics impress. Environments are richly detailed, from the dense forests and crumbling châteaux of Nazi-occupied France to coastal gun batteries and sprawling industrial complexes. The world feels alive and reactive, with a level of environmental fidelity that enhances immersion at every turn.

The storyline continues the tried-and-true formula of Karl Fairburne’s silent war behind enemy lines, but it does so with a sharp sense of purpose and urgency. Each mission is woven into a greater narrative that feels both personal and impactful — offering players a meaningful sense of progression and purpose.

Realism is one of Sniper Elite 5's most impressive achievements. Ballistics are deeply satisfying, with authentic bullet drop, wind resistance, and scope calibration. The iconic kill cam returns, more brutal and cinematic than ever, but never feels overused or gimmicky. It rewards patience and precision, two things the game constantly encourages.

The weapon variety is excellent, and each can be customized extensively. Whether you prefer a suppressed bolt-action rifle, an SMG for close encounters, or a silenced pistol for quiet kills, the game allows you to tailor your loadout to your playstyle. The gunplay is weighty, deliberate, and deeply rewarding.

What truly elevates Sniper Elite 5 is its replayability. Every campaign mission is set in a sprawling sandbox teeming with opportunities, alternate routes, hidden intel, and dynamic enemy behavior. I’ve replayed missions multiple times and still discover new vantage points, traps to exploit, and stealth paths I missed before. It’s a game that rewards exploration and experimentation — the more you play, the better and more strategic you become.

The difficulty settings are also worth praising. Whether you’re a casual player who just wants to enjoy the story or a hardcore tactician who craves authentic military simulation, Sniper Elite 5 scales beautifully to match your skill and preference.

Cons? I honestly don’t have any. The game delivers exactly what it sets out to do, and it does it with precision and polish.

Final Verdict:
Sniper Elite 5 is a tactical shooter done right — intelligent, engaging, and endlessly replayable. Whether you're a first-time sniper or a veteran of the franchise, this installment stands tall as the definitive Sniper Elite experience. Lock, load, and take the shot — you won’t regret it.

Fifth numbered installment of the Nazi ballbusting simulator. The game takes place in Vichy France, 1944, after Germany(SEV2, 1945), Africa(SE3, 1942), Italy(SE4, 1943) finally we got a (likely) final piece of the puzzle on Karl's WWII journey blowing up Wunderwaffes. The game remains all the same, empty lung, xray killcam, all the traps and shootings. The guy is a sniper, so the sniping is what he does. Done talking. And if you ever get tired of blasting German balls... For special guests we got the Japanese nuts to bust this time. Since you still can't commandeer vehicles you'll have to do a fair bit of legwork, but the game always throws a group of Nazis to kill along the way to ease your bore. Maps themselves could've been better though, as they feel often too restrictive, with paths blocked with uncrossable barbed wires and fences forcing players to make detours. Graphics, nothing groundbreaking. But its primitive, outdated antialiasing is problematic. It is almost non existent, tweaking between off and ultra has barely any difference. Nothing like distracting pixelated images to ruin the beauty of Mont Saint Michel and other pleasant landscapes of Francia. The game only offers FSR1 as its sole upscaler, so that also cannot be a help to smooth out the image. The base game has 8 missions which is on par with SE4 and SE3, technically there's a ninth one but that finale level lasts seconds to finish. Having both season passes adds 5 additional levels including the obligatory Hitler one. 

Like the previous games SE5 offers players weapon customization. And in my opinion, this hurts the game because of how extensive it is this time, rather than the lack thereof. Various options are present not only for rifles but also for every secondary and pistol, every major part of the gun tinkerable. With iron sights and scopes now available for weapons of all 3 slots, easy pinpoint precision is now possible with secondaries and sidearms, making rifles completely obsolete in a lot of situations. And once you unlock silencers, the game's difficulty dives faster than a Junkers Stuka divebomber. I know, it gives more freedom to players with their loadouts, and that's always good. But it inadvertently also created overpowered meta combinations that are objectively superior over others. If you value practicality over everything there's no reason for you to use most weapons provided. Reviews for all the DLC weapon packs are in mixed-mostly negative range also because of this I believe. They fail to differ. Why bother with other guns when a silenced, 6x scoped Strumgewehr 44 with damage clocked up to 11 with no scope glints can easily handle most tasks, with your trusty Karabiner 98 for occasional long range kills and armor?

With multiple starting spots, challenges and unlocks it encourages players to replay its levels several times... But the actual replayability? Not much. There's barely any deviation from your usual approach that can be made. The goals of the mission remain the same. All hostile NPCs are enemy personnel, thus viable targets, there is zero reason to sidestep and unnecessarily prolong the mission avoiding them. Just pick them all off, burst their heads, lungs, balls, or whatever. To inject some level of freshness into this routinely loop developers implemented an online mode that allows players to take the role of a Nazi sniper(technically, you can't play as a Nazi, all the crooked crosses in uniforms of playable Germans are censored) in others' games. As an invader you scan German NPCs to create your web of informants to track down the enemy infiltrator, and it's a good mechanic. I had a fair amount of fun in this mode gunning down newbies struggling to learn the ropes... But if both sides are actually competent, the mode quickly turns into a slog that often ends in the favor of the host(allied sniper) because of the focus mechanic, a closerange wallhack(this is disabled in authentic difficulty but hardcore players are rare) which can't be used by the invader.

It is a solid entry in the series that improves on its predecessor, especially for rifle enthusiasts. While it has some technical issues, the tactical stealth game play remains engaging: it's finally a chapter in which you actually sniper a lot, it's very satisfying. 

I played at "Sniper Elite" difficulty setting, the experience varies significantly with lower settings. I played on a 3060Ti, everything at ultra, 60fps rock solid. 

The Good:
- Significant improvement over the previous chapter with enhanced rifle mechanics
- Distinct weapon personalities - each firearm feels unique and satisfying
- Challenging AI on higher difficulties that actively tries to outflank and ambush you
- Excellent sound design - both immersive audio and realistic sound-based detection system
- Detailed, well-crafted scenarios that reward careful planning

The Bad:
- Animation invincibility frames: enemies become temporarily invulnerable during hit reactions
- Inconsistent damage model: some enemies are unrealistic bullet sponges
- Questionable weapon ballistics: completely wrong bullet drop calculations (e.g., 1911 pistol)
- Artificial level boundaries: visible areas blocked by arbitrary "mission area" restrictions instead of natural barriers

The Ugly:
- Sluggish controls: controls are horribly sluggish and often miss inputs. 

Conclusion:
Despite its flaws, this is a good tactical stealth game that series fans and newcomers alike will enjoy. The core sniping mechanics and improved AI make it worth playing, even if some technical issues can be frustrating sometimes.

Sniper Elite 5 marks a compelling evolution in the long-running stealth-action franchise, delivering a meticulously crafted World War II experience that blends tactical sniping, open-ended level design, and thrilling third-person combat. Building on the solid foundation of its predecessors, this installment refines the core gameplay mechanics with smarter AI, expanded player choice, and a sprawling campaign set primarily in occupied France, where resistance fighters seek to dismantle a secret Nazi superweapon project. The game shines most in its level design—large, detailed maps invite players to approach objectives with unparalleled freedom, whether by long-distance sniper shots, stealthy infiltration, or all-out combat. Each map is layered with verticality, numerous vantage points, and environmental hazards, encouraging creative strategies that reward patience and planning.

The signature bullet-cam mechanic returns, more cinematic than ever, offering satisfying slow-motion shots that track the bullet’s deadly path through bones and organs with graphic precision. This visceral feedback reinforces the game’s identity, delivering a uniquely brutal but oddly poetic form of violence that fans have come to expect. Beyond sniping, players can also employ a wide arsenal of WWII-era weapons and gadgets, with an improved customization system that allows meaningful tweaks to firearms’ performance and aesthetics. The stealth system is deeper too, with enemy patrols exhibiting more varied behavior and awareness, making silence and camouflage vital but never tedious.

Graphically, Sniper Elite 5 impresses with photorealistic environments, lifelike character models, and dynamic weather effects that influence visibility and gameplay tactics. The immersive audio design further elevates the tension—every distant gunshot, rustling leaf, and whispered radio chatter pulls players into the battlefield. The narrative, while not the game’s strongest suit, offers enough intrigue and character moments to keep the pace engaging, with performances that add weight to the resistance fighters’ plight without overshadowing the gameplay.

Multiplayer modes expand the game’s replayability significantly, featuring a range of competitive and cooperative options. The addition of an extensive mission creator and mod support empowers the community to build and share custom content, extending the title’s lifespan well beyond the main campaign. However, some players have noted occasional AI inconsistencies and minor bugs, particularly in stealth detection and pathfinding, though ongoing patches have addressed many issues promptly.

Overall, Sniper Elite 5 successfully balances accessibility and depth, offering a rich, rewarding experience for veterans and newcomers alike. Its combination of tactical freedom, brutal sniper combat, and immersive WWII settings makes it a standout entry in the genre, proving that the series still has plenty of precision and punch left to deliver. Whether stalking targets from hidden perches or engaging in tense close-quarters firefights, players will find in Sniper Elite 5 a nuanced and satisfying simulation of the deadly art of sniping.

Sniper Elite 5 is a great game—if you haven’t played any of the previous entries in the series. One feature I really enjoyed was the ability for players to invade each other’s games. It made co-op with my two friends a lot more engaging and added some unique, fun tension to our playthroughs. Beyond that, though, the improvements are pretty modest: slightly better graphics and larger maps.

Unfortunately, those larger maps don’t necessarily make for a better experience. Compared to Sniper Elite 4, the level design in SE5 feels more open—but not in a good way. SE4's maps had tighter pacing and more deliberate route design, which made missions feel more focused and satisfying. SE5’s openness often feels like it dilutes the gameplay, making it less immersive and a bit scattered.

To be clear, I’m comparing SE5 directly to its predecessor, because that’s the most relevant point of reference for me. If you’re new to the series, SE5 might be a great entry point. But for returning players, Sniper Elite 4 still feels like the better game overall.

Another major downside is the AI. It’s noticeably worse in SE5. I’m not sure what changes were made under the hood, but the AI behavior feels clunky and inconsistent—not just here, but also in Sniper Elite: Resistance. It’s a step backward.

Visually, the game is decently polished, but the graphics feel dated despite being a bit sharper than SE4. There’s also something off about the engine—it just doesn’t feel as refined or responsive, which affects the overall gameplay experience.

All things considered, I’d give Sniper Elite 5 a 5.5/10. Technically, I’d recommend it—but only if you’re buying it on sale. It’s not a bad game, but for fans of the series, it might feel more like a downgrade than a true sequel.

This game ended up being surprisingly more fun than I had previously thought. My previous experience being a bit of Sniper Elite 2 more than a decade ago. 

The highlight has to be invasions. Versing another player in a campaign environment adds a nice amount of tension to the experience as unlike AI, they cannot be exploited. The resulting cat and mouse game is incredibly fun. 
Being invaded, trying to sneak around and still complete objectives or setting up ambushes for the invader were incredible experiences. 
On the flip side, invading someone's game and trying to hunt them down with the limited resources and using map/objective knowledge to track them was a ton of fun.

I do think the experience for the campaign was better in authentic difficulty. Played most of the campaign in hard and then later switched to authentic (minus UI) and the lack of focus made the campaign and invasions both more tense. It almost feels like cheating using focus mode to keep track of the invader to be honest. The white silhouettes especially are the big culprit.

The campaign overall was great and I enjoyed all the maps. Some of the maps like Spy Academy and Landing Force were definite standouts. There are a multitude of ways to accomplish objectives, so there's good replay value there.

Multiplayer I've barely touched but it seems fun. I'll keep the game installed to mess around in plus to invade other players' games.

Visuals and soundtrack are quite good. The game has a nice aesthetic and a couple of the grand soundtracks sound epic. 

Only had minor nitpicks, mostly to do with ledges and equivalents. The player can sometimes just ignore them and fall. Trying to aim over them also mixes inputs leaving you hanging when you do not want to. 

Also, I think each time the player dies, there should be a killcam showing where the final bullet came from. This is especially needed in invasions where it only comes into play sometimes.

Overall, I highly recommend this game to anyone who wants a bit of stealth action. The game succeeds at the experience it is trying to sell. 9/10

The latest addition to the mainline Sniper Elite series, though at the time of this review it had been out for quite some time. If you know and love the series, you'll get mostly the same deal here as you did with the previous installments. You get to visit interesting locations and shoot nasty people in nasty places from afar to stop the aforementioned nasties from cooking up some kind of super weapon that will surely win them the war. I personally prefer the more challenging previous installment, but this is a good time regardless. Get to it! Oh, and do check out Axis Invasion mode!

If you are unfamiliar with the series, you play as Karl Fairburne an OSS sniper during WW2, and this time you are deployed to France, around the time of the allied invasion, to investigate and stop a Nazi plot: operation Kraken. This all unfolds in the span of 8 missions of the main campaign, where you have to make your way through spacious open levels that have you tackle various primary and secondary objectives before extracting.
The main staple of the series is sniping your enemies - you never would have guessed. Your kill shots trigger a bullet camera and x-ray shots of the victim on impact. Gross, satisfying and it really never gets old. The rifle is supposed to be your weapon of choice, but you also carry a submachine gun and pistol and you can melee kill enemies as well. Unfortunately, in my opinion, sniping takes more of a backseat to stealth killing by way of the latter two options. That is if you go for a stealth approach, which is how this game naturally plays for most people, I would guess. You can definitely go loud all the way as well, but that's not where the gameplay shines and I don't really enjoy that play style myself.
You’ll level up and unlock new skills throughout the campaign, and the same goes for weapons and modifications for those weapons. This time around there are a lot of those modifications. Most of them have clear advantages and drawbacks and it's up to you to assemble a kit that you feel matches your play style best. Being a stealth player myself, I tend to favor modifications like suppressors and stuff that increases aim stability.

In addition to the campaign there are also other modes, like surviving against waves of AI enemies on various maps of the campaign and from the multi-player mode. Speaking of which, yes there is also multi-player, with modes like Team Match and No-Cross. I like team match the best, but fair warning: toxicity ahead.

Though by far the best mode in the game is Axis Invasion. It is simply the single best idea that Rebellion has every included in any of their Sniper Elite games. If enabled, and to be clear it is fully optional, this allows another player to invade your campaign missions as an enemy sniper, adding a lot more challenge to the game. It's fun to play from both perspectives, but I must admit I like playing as the invader the most. 
Theoretically. Mostly. You see there's a huge drawback to the mode, being that the invader is at really big disadvantage in all difficulties except the hardest one: Authentic. Otherwise the campaign player will be able to gauge your approximate direction / location at all times using focus-mode, be able to spot you though walls using focus mode, and be able to shoot you thru most cover (including brick walls) with armor piercing rounds. Naturally, there are unfortunately plenty of players that abuse this just to grief invaders, and it often turns what should be a fun cat-and-mouse game, into boredom and frustration. Also, beware of players the load into missions that have been cleared of AI enemies and that are full of lethal traps for the invader, using stacked mines, TNT and whatnot. So A+ for the idea, but the execution leaves a lot to be desired. In my experience, the best way to engage with this mode is as the campaign player on Authentic difficulty.

Some final words on technical issues I’ve experienced. The Easy Anti-Cheat included in the game can seemingly mess up at anytime and remove you from online play, whether that is a mode like Team Match or Axis Invasion. General stability has also been an issue for me, with regular crashes to desktop, unsure what the problem is there. Finally, the game is by no means free of minor bugs and jank, which will seemingly at this point never be fixed.

Set against the backdrop of World War II in France, the game immerses players in a meticulously crafted environment filled with stealth action, tactical gameplay. As a sniper named [i][b]Karl Fairburne[/b][/i], players are tasked with taking down high-profile targets and sabotaging enemy operations, all while navigating through designed maps that encourage exploration and strategy.

[h3]GAMEPLAY MECHANICS[/h3]
[i][b]Sniper Elite 5[/b][/i] builds on the established formula of its predecessors, offering a blend of stealth and sniping mechanics. The game introduces refined mechanics for movement and shooting, allowing for more fluid gameplay. Players can utilise various tools at their disposal, including a wide array of weapon modifications, traps, and distractions to outmaneuver enemies. The addition of new traversal methods, such as climbing and vaulting, enhances verticality in gameplay, enabling players to find optimal sniping spots or stealth routes.

One of the standout features of the game is the emphasis on tactical planning. Maps are expansive and cleverly designed, providing multiple pathways and opportunities for players to approach missions differently. This encourages creativity and experimentation, offering a rewarding experience for those who enjoy calculating their next move with precision. Additionally, the return of the iconic slow-motion X-ray kill cam showcases the visceral impact of long-range shots, enhancing the sense of satisfaction when executing a perfect sniping technique.

[h3]VISUALS[/h3]
Graphically, [i][b]Sniper Elite 5[/b][/i] is a remarkable achievement, showcasing detailed environments that reflect the wartime setting. From lush countryside to ruined cities, each location is intricately designed. Lighting effects, weather variations, and dynamic shadows contribute to an immersive atmosphere, while character models and animations enhance the visual fidelity of the experience. It also includes [i][b]ultra-wide[/b][/i] support, where you can spot those sneaky Nazis lurking in the corners of your vision.

[h3]AUDIO[/h3]
The sound design complements the visuals perfectly; the sounds of gunfire, environment, and even the subtle strategising of the battlefield create a rich auditory experience. Voice acting adds depth to the narrative, bringing life to the characters while conveying the tension and stakes of the missions.

[h3]NARRATIVE[/h3]
While [i][b]Sniper Elite 5[/b][/i] emphasises gameplay mechanics, its story offers enough intrigue to keep players engaged. The narrative revolves around thwarting Nazi plans in France, with [i][b]Karl Fairburne[/b][/i] facing off against formidable foes. The storyline, while not overly complex, is delivered through dynamic cinematics and mission briefings that add context and motivation to the gameplay.

[h3]ATMOSPHERE[/h3]
The atmosphere has been enhanced with inspiration from real historical settings, locations, and weaponry, immersing players in the gritty realities of war. This attention to detail elevates the experience and provides players with a sense of connection to the period.

[h3]MULTIPLAYER[/h3]
[i][b]Sniper Elite 5[/b][/i] expands its offerings with a robust multiplayer component, featuring cooperative and competitive modes. The ability to team up with friends for shared objectives enhances the overall experience, allowing for collaborative strategising. The inclusion of a unique PvPvE mode, where players can compete against one another while dealing with AI enemies, adds an exciting twist that keeps the gameplay fresh and unpredictable.

[h3]REPLAYABILITY[/h3]
The game's structure encourages replayability, with various challenges, collectibles, and unlockable content waiting to be discovered. Different difficulty levels and customisable options allow players to tailor their experience, making it suitable for both sniping newcomers and series veterans alike.

[h3]THE LOWDOWN[/h3]
Overall, [i][b]Sniper Elite 5[/b][/i] is a worthy addition to the franchise, successfully balancing engaging gameplay, good visuals, and an immersive atmosphere. Its combination of tactical shooting and stealth mechanics offers a rewarding experience for players who relish strategic gameplay. While the narrative may not be groundbreaking, it serves its purpose well by providing context for the action. Additionally, the game features robust multiplayer options and high replayability.

Whether you’re a skilled marksman or entirely new to the sniper genre, this game has something for everyone, making it an impressive addition to the world of tactical shooters. If you’re ready to embrace your inner sharpshooter and take down enemies from a distance, grab your gear and prepare to snipe your way through World War II with a smile. Just remember: it’s more than just a game; it’s a fantastic excuse to don your camouflage pyjamas!

I played Sniper Elite 4 back in January and absolutely loved it. I waited for the Steam Summer Sale and grabbed the full game, honestly the main campaign is worth the full price, but I wouldn’t say the DLCs are. The DLC maps feel either uninspired or empty, adding little to the overall experience. So unless you're after special weapons or skins, the best value is to buy the main game solo.

For gameplay, the mechanics feel similar to the previous game, the battlefield has moved from Italy to France. At first you're limited to regular ammo, but as progress there will be non-lethal, suppressed, armor-piercing rounds, which are useful for quieter takedowns or vehicles. Since you can't keep enough ammo to fully clear a map, you’ll need to scavenge from enemies or search workbenches (which also offer weapon upgrades), unless you play stealth pass or melee kills. But after all Sniper Elite is all about taking out Nazis, not like Splinter Cell or Hitman franchise where the focus is on avoiding kills. That said, I find it odd that the system scores higher for knocking Nazis unconscious instead of killing them. But I reached max level 40 before starting the last main campaign, so it seems playstyle doesn’t matter in the end.

Speaking of level up, I recommend fully exploring maps. Most optional missions won’t appear until you're close to the mission area or gathered enough intel. You'll also need tools like a wrench, bolt cutter and crowbar to infiltrate certain areas, and most importantly, dynamite for destroying safe doors, AA guns or Panzers. While Instinct highlights these tools, you’ll still need to get close to locate them.

My favorite map is Spy Academy. It offers a fantastic sniper spot near the camp, allowing a great view of the entire basilica-town across a long bridge. With a long range, big scope powerful rifle, empty the clip is incredibly satisfying, and I earned the 500+ meter shot medal. Just be patient, and manage the bullet drop. As you pass the bridge or go underneath it, the sea-shore town is filled with details, there are always multiple paths to explore. This map is like some of the Italy maps from the previous game, and the basilica (Spy Academy) is a stunning Gothic structure. The stained glass inside looks amazing when you climb to the top and enter photo mode, and the flying buttresses outside are excellent. The level encourages thorough exploration as the meeting point is located in a room at the top of the basilica, making it nearly impossible to miss the beauty of the architecture . The exit point is located in a joint church, I ended up replaying it more than twice because of how enjoyable it was.

Other maps are more focused on armory than cities, with missions in metal melting factories, rocket bases, navy submarines...These aren’t as appealing to me, the sabotage missions feel tedious especially when waypoints are unclear. I particularly dislike missions that require locating people, unless I go loud and attract Nazis, the targets always wander randomly around the map.

Regarding difficulty, I started on Normal then switched to Hard. The AI seems easier than in the previous game, with longer reaction times and less intelligence, and it’s not fun shooting at dummy. That said, Authentic difficulty (highest level) is too much for me, mainly because I can’t see the hit points in the scope.

My complaints are (1) Karl can only carry one rifle, yet he is able to carry one extra big gun like a submachine gun or a shotgun. It would be perfect for dual rifle gameplay - one quieter for short range killing and one badass long range louder rifle that can kill over 500 meters. (2) Panzerfaust not a default weapon. (3) Logo in photo mode doesn't work.

The most frustrating issue I encountered was in the Secret Weapon mission. Near the end of the game, I ran into a game-breaking bug where the cutscene wouldn’t trigger at the goal point. It kept saying, "Did we miss something? Where is Moller?" and I had to restart the level. I think I ran into a similar bug in the Wolf Mountain DLC.

I finished and replayed the main campaign and all 4 DLC maps in 22 hours on hard difficulty. Despite the bugs and the underwhelming DLCs, it’s still a solid game. I recommend it especially when it's on sale.

Almost the perfect Sniper Elite Game... Almost.

Sniper Elite 5 is a game I had been looking forward to while playing through the series, mainly because it takes place in France and it is by far my favorite Theatre of War in WWII.
And while I was pleasantly surprised and had a TON of fun with the game, putting pretty much the most hours into this title than the rest of the franchise, I was left amazed but at the same time baffled at the changes made in this game.

So let us start with the positives.

- Invasion Mode. This is THE gamechanger for me, an absolute stroke of genius by Rebellion!
In Invasion Mode you have the chance to be invaded by an enemy player whose job it is to hunt you down, or you can do so yourself to other Karls out there.
This mode has single-handedly made the game 200 times more fun for me, because it fundamentally changed the way that I played the game and approached every objective; I'd survey the terrain, start putting traps in important bottlenecks or booby traps on soldiers with the knowledge that at ANY time, somebody could come for me, and it has made for some great moments where I would start an alert and as if clockwork, get invaded at the same time, leading to a lot of panicked running and hiding while trying to dispatch my pursuers before the Invader catches up and has me dead to rights.
Or the times where I was able to take out an invader because he stuck his head out of his little cover for just a second too long, allowing me to get that perfect headshot on him.
The reverse is also true, where I outmaneuver a Karl in such a way that I am no longer where he thinks I am, only to pop up behind him with a knife in his back, or flank him and give him a shot to the side of the head.

These moments MADE Sniper Elite 5 for me, and I could no longer imagine playing without the mode (Unless im just going for challenges and achievments since I finished the game now.)

- Spy Academy & Secret Weapon. Both these levels are PHENOMENAL and Spy Academy in particular to me is considered the peak in Level Design within the Sniper Elite series so far, no level comes close to the amount of fun I had traversing it. Secret Weapon is also notable for just the sheer amount of length I spent on it, clocking in at around 3 hours of playtime on my first run through the map, including several invaders coming for me throughout which was a blast!

- The weapons as usual feel incredible, and the art of -learning- your rifle, how it performs, how your shots are affected and mastering it, are a great deal of fun!

- Vehicles are more threatening. In SE4 it was very easy to just snipe into the slits of vehicles to take out driver and/or gunner, which made the vehicles quite easy to deal with and formulaic. You make sure to take out around it first and then you have free reign to bully it. While vehicles are still somewhat easy to deal with, they require a lot more work to take down. Slits are gone and the most reliable way is to use a satchel charge on the back and then fire away at the engine of each vehicle.

So then, let me get into some of the nitpicks I have with the game:

- In SE4, missions sometimes had enemies fighting with Resistance members, that is gone. Why? This was a great deal of fun, using the firefight to flank around and get a bead on the Nazis was so much fun in 4, why did it not return here?

- In SE4, the levels were either wonderful and blow me away, or awful (Monastery, Inception). While the Levels in SE5 are more average, the design is more consistently good across the board. The only mission I outright disliked ended up being the War Factory because of the way it literally railroads (pun not intended) you into paths, and most of the level taking place inside buildings.
Also where are all the Sniper Nests? The rooftops? In SE4 missions like the Dockyard and Inception you were able to enter buildings and go up to rooftops, cranes and all sorts of places. Where are my overlooking areas like the start of San Celini? Most of this is missing in SE5 and there is just a huge lack of any real sniper nests in a game called SNIPER Elite
And even when you find a Snipers Nest, the only enemies you are able to snipe from your limited view (be it a window or a ton of trees around) are only 50-100m away... Where the hell are my 300-500m snipes at? I have to go out of my way to position myself to get those sometimes.

Sniper Elite 5 is the biggest leap forward for the series yet, fixing many of the clunky mechanics that held past games back. The controls are so much smoother—movement no longer feels stiff, aiming is more responsive, and the new animations make every action, from climbing to melee kills, look and feel more natural. The sniping itself is the best it's ever been, with improved ballistics and those gloriously brutal X-ray kill cams returning in all their gory detail.

The levels are bigger and more dynamic, rewarding exploration and creative takedowns, and the invasion mode adds a thrilling unpredictability to the campaign. That said, the AI still has its dumb moments, stealth can be inconsistent, and the story is as bland as ever. Multiplayer and co-op are fun but don’t redefine the experience.

If you bounced off older Sniper Elite games due to jank, this one might win you over. It’s polished, more immersive, and a clear upgrade—but it’s still not quite a must-play outside of its niche.

As a fans of this game, written so many reviews for this franchise for a decade now since the reboot of Sniper Elite, I think 5 is still true to its root, a WW2 sniper shooting game with our failure Austrian artist as a staple DLC to the franchise and gameplay improvement every installments.

People might criticize that this game barely change from Elite 4, Italian Campaign, but I disagree. Being a person who put nearly 30-40 hrs in 4, 5 improved a lot of QoL and AI (more on this later). 
More variety of ammunition to choose from. Apart from Subsonic introduced in 4, there are Match, Armor piecing (as some players said that it was too easy to kill vehicles/tanks in previous installments so there you have it), non-fatal and soft point are debuted in this game.

The map design also improved on what makes the charm for Elite 4. It connects the each zone together which is better than 4 imo which basically like many sandboxes connected together to form 1 map.

Gunplays a lot better now. You can aim down sight on the iron sight now so no more rage inducing where you have to switch left & right to aim the guy with SMG/Pistol.

Customization also improved. Back in 4, I barely customized my weapon, just one time and done. With 5, you have to adapt with the situations.

So it's all sunshine and rainbow from 4 to 5?

Not quite.

Like I mentioned the AI, it's smarter that's for sure but sometimes it's more annoying now as it's harder to shake them off or reduce the awareness to normal. It's quite a challenge for veteran or seasoned players but for the one that's new to the series this would be annoying. I think this is one of the reason why I refunded at the first time.

Second, the maps. There's a lot more plain field or urban compared to Italian's slope and mountain in 4 so that's why it's a lot more challenging than previous one.

Third, customization plays a lot more factor in here than previous installments, meaning you have to spend time to find the best one for you. While you can find the workbench in the field, I encourage any player to test in the shooting range than in the mission as you have to stick with that setup until you can find the workbench which a lot of the time doesn't appear on the maps until you walk into the zone.

Mentioning that, I think the "detecting" important zone/area (basically sub-mission) are worse than 4 despite being more realistic. You have to loot the body or eavesdropping what soldier said (you can use the binocular, zoom in and listening to them despite being like hundreds of meter far away) to get the intel/insight where you should headed. This is not for anyone who's going gun blazing as you will absolutely missed a lot of opportunity to finish sub-missions.

Talking about sub-missions, You have to finish these tasks to unlock more guns and customization. My first 6 hours into the game, I only used the starting weapon in the game until I realized I have to finish tasks to unlock the rest.

Btw, they changed the looting system from switching your weapon permanently, you only temporary pick and use it. The second you switch to your 2ndary or sidearms, that weapon will drop. This is somehow annoying as the game should encourage you to find better sniper rifles by hunting other snipers and pick their rifles to unlock that setup. This is a missed opportunity, sadly.

Lastly, the invasion system. It's basically a PVP mode that you can allow other players to join in your campaign mission (or invading others), posing as whatever you want from plain cloth officers, soldiers to elite snipers in a ghillie suit. Your only task is to kill the invader/other players. 
It might sounds good to hear but I think you can imagine how bad this can turn out to be. There are systems to prevent people from camping and stuff but the fact is nobody wants to play this mode. The toggle to turn off the invasion also doesn't encourage anyone to toggle it on. The rewards are quite interesting as many characters/customizations are behind the invasion rewards but I guess with how the game has already passed its peak I probably wouldn't be able to unlock it forever.

Overall.
The same old sniper elite, as usual. Improved gameplay and slightly better story (may not be everyone cup of tea). Despite some odd decisions from developers, this game is still recommended. But with their decisions or monetization lately (both this and dead war), I guess it's mostly recommendable only if it's on sales.

I've always believed a good sniper game is about far more than steady aim and long distance shots. It’s a test of strategy, patience, and adaptability. This latest installment strikes that balance impressively, offering missions that invite diverse playstyles. Whether I chose silent infiltration, carefully timed sniper eliminations, or full-scale firefights, each tactic delivered its own genuine satisfaction. Interestingly though, a direct and aggressive approach often rewarded me with more points—a subtle nudge, perhaps, to embrace action over finesse.

Mission design itself proved consistently engaging, each location distinct enough to maintain interest and tactical creativity from start to finish. Visually, in sharp 4K detail, the environments truly come to life, immersing me convincingly in wartime settings. Controls never felt cumbersome, allowing precision when I needed it most.

My only real gripe was the music, which felt repetitive at times, fading into a predictable background loop rather than adding to the mission’s tension. It wasn't distracting, but it wasn't memorable either.

Ultimately, what stood out was the game's ability to encourage strategic freedom without punishing experimentation. It's the kind of experience that quietly respects your intelligence while entertaining your instincts. Exactly what I look for when I take aim at my next target.

Of course, the iconic X-ray kill cam is back and better than ever. Watching a perfectly placed shot travel in slow motion before hitting its target with bone-crushing impact never gets old. It adds a deeply satisfying element to every sniper kill, making precision shots even more rewarding.

With its gripping campaign, enjoyable multiplayer modes, and rich replayability, Sniper Elite 5 is an excellent choice for fans of tactical shooters and stealth gameplay. Whether you're playing solo or with friends, it offers countless hours of thrilling, strategic action.

I got sniper elite 5 a few days ago, and I don't see it getting much recognition. I'll admit, when I first started it, I had mixed feelings. It's very clear that the game took heavy inspiration from Hitman, and at first, I was worried that the game would suck, that the developers had given up on it, and were just trying to cash in on a successful game. I played it further, and was really pleasantly surprised.

First, I'll put it into context. Sniper elite is a stealth game with a heavy emphasis on sniping, with x-ray cams when you kill enemies. Originally, SE was a very linear game, but as the series went on, the level design got more and more open with each game, but I think didn't truly blossom until the fourth entry to the series.

Sniper Elite 5 took what made sniper elite 4 good, and then slapped on a lot of the stuff that made hitman good, and the result is this really addictive open level structure where you're encouraged to go back and explore the same giant levels several times over, getting tangible rewards for doing so, but not restricting how you do it in the same way that hitman did. Don't get me wrong, I love Hitman, but I felt like some of the tasks and challenges in it got so specific that it felt less open than it actually was.

Sniper Elite has TONS of optional objectives per map, and you get rewards for doing them. But these optional objectives are set up so that you can usually do them in a multitude of ways, rather than following a script to do it. As an example, I'm only on the 3rd mission after around a week, because I've been doing the second level to unlock stuff I want. I realized you could unlock a suppressor for the 1911 pistol, which is semi-automatic, unlike the pump action pistol you start with. But then I didn't like the weapon sway. So I did optional stuff to unlock the carbine kit for the pistol. And then I learned you could convert it to 22 caliber, making it even more quiet. So once again, I went through the level, did a challenge tk unlock that. Then i unlocked a rifle I'd missed in the level, by playing it again, only to decide the rifle had too much weapon sway. So now I'm trying to unlock stuff for that rifle.

It's an absolutely addictive gameplay loop. And each map is big enough that whenever i replay them, I find new routes, or secret passages.

But i think the most important part of all of this is that you don't even have to play it as a stealth game. It steers you in that direction, obviously. But you're not really punished if you're seen - there's no "right" way to do it. The punishment is having to deal with whoever else goes after you. Or leaving a trail behind if another player invades your game (which you can turn off if you like). So if you're able to blow a truck up and get away before they see you, or machine gun your way through a corridor of Nazis, you don't get penalized for using loud options. It takes away the frustration that you'd normally get from grinding a game like Hitman for unlocks, because you can kind of just do it however you want, and with each replay of a mission, you've got a new route to try, or a new weapon you just unlocked, or the option to have a friend help you. I love Hitman, but my issue is I find myself grinding and grinding with the same loadout every single time until I get what I want. In SE, I feel like I'm not restricted from using all of these gadgets I've unlocked.

To start with, I have played the previous installments (Sniper Elite 2, 3, 4 and their zombie spin-offs) and, compared with its predecessors, [b]Sniper Elite 5 feels almost like the ultimate package so far.[/b]

[i]This review will be only based on the single-player part of the game as I haven't touched either the 'Axis Invasion' or 'Multiplayer' modes.[/i]

The campaign maps are massive and give you plenty of freedom. You are basically dropped into a semi-open world area for each mission where they give you multiple objectives (main and secondary ones, only the main ones are mandatory) and also more than one way to tackle them. Let's say you have to destroy a generator, you can either blow it up with explosives or cut out the wires that powers it up. Or maybe you have to clear out a checkpoint of soldiers, this can be done stealthily up close, rushing in guns-blazing or also far away from a sniper spot. Besides, there's usually more than one way to reach your objective, whether is it through climbing or finding a secret locked door (in which you have to find the key beforehand with one of the soldiers or around the door area) or tunnels. Something worth mentioning about the campaign is that, if you play with minimal to no HUD (like I did for my entire playthrough), the protagonist gives you clues/hints or updates you about new objectives that you encounter in the field which can be amazingly helpful when you combine it with the in-game map to check out your mission progress. Just remember to not rush the campaign. As the maps are huge, take your time. Try to do missions stealthily, explore as much as you can so you can discover various collectibles, exotic weapons, items, etc. Enjoy what each map has to offer as they were undoubtedly beautifully crafted.

Even though the campaign mode is wonderfully made, [b]one downside for me would be the customization[/b]. And why is that? As I've mentioned before, the maps are massive and obviously filled with collectibles, intel for objectives and there are also the 'workbenches' which works like a 'loadout switcher' during the mission. However, you have to find these 'workbenches' around the map to unlock more attachments for your weapons (suppressors, gun barrels, grips, etc). So, in case you finish your main mandatory objectives and want to exfiltrate but missed one of these workbenches, you'll have to replay the mission later and find them and unlock any desired attachments. Despite that, even though the weapons arsenal is significantly smaller than previous sniper elites, you can greatly customize your main sniper, secondary weapon and pistol. During each mission, you can also carry a 'temporary weapon' (dropped weapons, basically) and they don't replace your main weapons that you've chosen before the mission.

As for difficulty, I love that it is 100% customizable. You can have super intelligent enemies that flank you constantly and are not bullet spongy or overly accurate, which is usually what the 'hard difficulties' are disguised of and all about. You can also customize the 'sniper shooting' experience (gravity and wind) and also the hud. For my playthrough, I set the HUD to minimal (used the in-game map to guide myself, it's the classic 'M' key on your keyboard), disabled the empty lung assistance indicator (where the shot would land, basically), activated gravity impact and disabled the wind effects. As for the enemies, I set them to be overly experienced/intelligent but not bullet spongy. This way, they would spot me easily, flank me, but once we engaged out of stealth, I could take them down easily if my awareness and reaction times were on point. Furthermore, when it came to tanking bullets, I did not change this option, I kept it on default. To me, this made the game fun and challenging, it had a great balance between both. It wasn't overly easy but it wasn't also superbly difficult that it would ruin the fun.

Character movement is certainly an improvement. In Sniper Elite 4, the protagonist would move around too slowly (even when crouched) and that kind of ruined the fun for me. Now in SE5, the character walks around a bit faster and movement is much more fluid.

Weapons as a whole feel great and the gun sounds are also on point. To my mind, the gunplay in shooting games need to have its fair share of realistic sounds and weapon feel otherwise the game feels bland and the guns feel that they are made out of plastic. Thankfully, this doesn't happen here. Guns are loud and heavy as they are supposed to be. Landing headshots from far far away is deeply satisfying and it truly makes you feel somewhat like a real sniper.

Graphics are outstandingly great here, you have its fair share of places to go and climb and enjoy the view for some beautiful screenshots. On the other hand, they were not the selling point for me. I guess the gameplay itself counted much more at the end of the day.

Would I recommend Sniper Elite 5? Obviously! If you are a hardcore fan of the series, simply go for it! As mentioned previously, Sniper Elite 5 combines all the elements from its predecessors and tries to create the ultimate sniping experience for you. 
In case you are still unsure, wait for a sale. Just don't sleep on this game, you certainly won't be disappointed.

[h1]Sniper Elite 5: Stealth, Strategy, and... Testicle Shots[/h1]
Sniper Elite 5 is the game where you get to take out Nazis—one precision shot at a time—while secretly wishing you could do it in the most awkward way possible.

Gameplay:
You’re a super stealthy sniper, blending in with the shadows, waiting for the perfect moment to take down your target. But let’s be real, you’ll spend more time lining up your shot to accidentally blow up a barrel, sending everything into chaos. The real fun, though? The slow-motion X-ray cam that shows off your perfectly timed shot... and sometimes, a perfectly timed shot to the testicles. Yes, you can literally shoot the enemy where it hurts most. And yes, it’s hilarious every single time.

Stealth:
It’s all about sneaking around, taking out bad guys without them noticing. Unless you accidentally knock over a bottle or fire your gun like a maniac. But really, who needs stealth when you can just blow up the entire base with one well-placed grenade?

Multiplayer:
Just imagine coordinating with friends to set up the perfect sniper shot. Then, one of them blows it by yelling “I GOT HIM!” and ruining the stealthy silence.

In Sniper Elite 5, nothing’s more satisfying than a well-executed shot... especially when it hits the family jewels. It’s like the game’s way of saying, “Yes, you are a master sniper... and yes, this is funny.”

I sometimes wish Steam had a middle of the road option for reviewing games because while Sniper Elite 5 isn't a terrible game, it's clearly a downgrade in what made Sniper Elite 4 very fun. Allow me to explain.

Sniper Elite 5 takes pride in itself in a few ways. One such pride is with its campaign's maps being very large. They are very welcoming to exploration and in a sense, adventure. There is no pressure against the player, you aren't timed as you move around, allowing to find all the little nooks and crannies as you move through these maps. Depending on the difficulty you want to play on, the game can easily make you feel pressured though, but that is entirely up to you in the end. So what's the problem then?

The major flaw with SE5 is its "expanded sandbox experience". While on first glance, it seems pretty welcoming with how you can approach enemies and dealing with them. It as a whole is a huge downgrade in interaction. An example of this is how Karl can knock out enemies, while neat and an interesting way to play pacifist, it becomes a double edged sword when a single guard you happened to miss wanders about and discovered the knocked out buddy and wakes him back up. But hey, there is a way to prevent this and keep your pacifist way right? Well there are those yellow supply chest, seemingly inspired by Hitman where you can store up to two enemies in them to effectively keep them out of the fight for the remaining part of your mission. There is also the tall grass too, which works just as well funny enough.

But the issue isn't how Karl takes down enemies in pacifistic way, its how he approaches them lethally. One of the huge flaws in this game which confused me was how the player approaches enemies in a more lethal sniper format. Now you can just point and click on the head, sure, but in the previous games you had the ability to target a grenade on an enemy's uniform or belt, causing it to explode, creating a distraction as well as panic among enemies. 90% of enemies in this game don't have grenades physically equipped to their belts anymore which is odd since they throw them like candy when they do spot you. 

Another large downgrade is the approach to vehicle combat, in this game weapon customization is a very strong boon the player has and the ability to make a suppressed anti-armor rifle is pretty neat, but the interaction between vehicles and the player is extremely limited. The very first level, Atlantikwall introduces you to vehicle patrols right after you complete the tutorial piece of the game and again, at first its pretty neat seeing a traveling patrol of trucks, wagens and bikes roaming around the maps (until it breaks, I'll get that towards the end of the review), but targeting of vehicle weakpoints is extremely hit or miss in SE5, even with Anti-Armor ammo, sometimes it takes up to two, four shots before you blow up a troop truck, even a wagen. Later in the same level, you encounter the first major flaw of this issue, the patrol boat. On the water in front of the beach bunkers is a boat with spotlight and turret.

In previous games, you could target the driver AND gunner of the boat, but in SE5 only the spotlight can be broken and the driver can be killed. The gunner can't be targeted at all and even looking at the gunner position reveals there is no visible soldier there, just a rotating empty combat position with a gun that seems to be alive on its own or operating via remote control. Its weird. Same thing applies to the Armored Car, the Sd. Kfz 222, its driver can be killed but for some reason, unlike SE4, the gunner can't be targeted at all. The same can be said of the Tiger II tank enemy where you can't even kill the driver or gunner. Its just a strange and odd choice of sandbox limitations given how "expanded" its suppose to be.

But now that I got my personal gripes out of the way, lets talk about the real reason why you should only buy it if you just want to play Sniper Elite. The bugs and the DLC consumer model. Oh golly. The bugs in this game are extremely visible and from what I've noticed, there has been little to zero attempt to fix them. In my 100+ hours of play, I've seen so many strange and odd bugs regarding the sandbox and how the AI interacts with it. Again, jump back to the first level, Atlantikwall again. One of the secondary objectives is blowing up a series of three Flak 38 emplacements (fun fact two enemies incorrectly call the 38s, 88s in their dialogue for some reason, another oddity moment), now its pretty straightforward, you blow up the first one and the second one without issue, its the last one by the Naval Cannon objective that breaks the game's sandbox. Upon blowing up that AA gun, enemies by the nearby road will come over to investigate and even some vehicle patrols will stop, hop out and investigate as well, but that's the issue. They will never stop investigating, leaving on your mini-map a strangely permanent mark of investigation. Even after all the enemies are dead or knocked out, it will not remove the mark.

This causes so many issues, no matter how far away you are. Enemies will stop reacting to your Whistle tool and reset their pathing, throwing a Bottle will aggro any enemies on the spot regardless if you are across the way, they'll know where you are at and open fire on your exact position. Vehicle pathing breaks as vehicles will stop in strange spots, get stuck and remain like this. The whole thing just breaks entirely and this happens on every single map. Its a "sandbox" problem and just from a glance, it seems be literally the AI unable to restore itself back to a normal pattern. It gets stuck, completely flubbing up how your mission flows as a result. Its bizarre.

Now then, the other reason why you should be wary. The DLC consumer model. Its bad. Its really bad. 10$ for a weapon and skin pack? 15$ for a single mission and weapon pack? It really screams money grubbing given the fact the maps are weirdly smaller and more compact compared to the base game content. The ONLY pack that is actually worth the 10$ is Kraken Awakens, given that its mission is placed on a decently big map and it properly wraps up the final strings on the campaign's story.

But what about the shooting funny mustache man DLC (Wolf Mountain DLC)? My disappoint is extreme and very depressing, this is one of the most bugged things I've ever seen. While the map is not as large as others, it has a lot of flow problems (ie, only one way to get to the main structure, through the tunnel where vehicle patrols come through commonly as example). On top of that Mr. H's AI is extremely broken. For some reason 90% of the game, he'll be standing in the open (spawned there) or just in sitting in his staff car not moving or doing anything. His bike escorts also seemingly stuck in place too (after peeking under the game's hood, it seems his front bike escort driver isn't even loaded properly most of the time; usually characters assigned to a mission have a set name and a bio. The rear bike escort does have this and on rare moments when the mission actually works, the front bike driver ALSO has a set name and bio, but if the driver is listed as "Unknown Soldier" aka a temporary soldier spawned in for vehicle patrolling, the mission breaks entirely; this is your reason right here). The fact that there was never a bug fix or addressing of this issue should tell you a lot about SE5 and its problems. There are other things but for me, gameplay and just general flow are my major points of frustration.

In the end however, it's a decently good game marred by a lot of issues and a lot more bugs. A lot of questionable downgrades as well, but I do find myself enjoying the whole sneaking around the maps, and self imposed challenges I gave myself as I play it. Regardless, its one of those games where you should think about before you buy. If you do wanna play it, I'd suggest waiting for a sale.

Some of the enemy snipers are annoying because if they even remotely spot you, they'll just start shooting endlessly at the location you last were, giving your location away, even though they have 0 confirmation that something was actually there. Operation Führer, which is a massive part of the appeal to sniper elite games, killing the man himself, was a painful map, not much sniping opportunities, constantly having vehicles drive past making any kills immediately visible. Sniper Elite 5 is a third person/first person hybrid shooter, where you are deployed in locations across Europe during World War II as, you guessed it, an elite sniper. With a decent array of weapons to choose from and customize with unlock-able extensions and attachments, it is another solid entry in the Sniper Elite series of video games. I have always enjoyed the series, from the zombie titles, to the straight forward shoot Nazi's themes, and would recommend this game to anyone who enjoys a mission oriented shooter with a variety of strategy options. 

You can choose to confront the enemies, have the alarms blare and take everyone on as they come, or you can do what I do, which is sneak around, mask the sound of my gun with any nearby masking source, and snipe people from as far away as possible. If not, I pull out a silenced pistol and ensure nobody finds the body and raised the alarm. 

There is a decent amount of missions in the base game, with a load of areas and secondary objectives to complete. The DLCs are underwhelming in terms of content, but I did pick up the Season One pass for the extra missions and completed them, out of obligation really. In addition to the missions, you can do some single player modes like 'endless' which is defending a location from a number of enemy waves, and there is a deep and natural ability to coop the missions and modes with a friend, which I highly recommend!

While I didn't partake in the multiplayer options, there is a variety of options in terms of gameplay, including 'Axis Invasion', where an online player joins your mission to try to stop you from completing it, which is a very cool concept. Standard deathmatch-like and other modes are also available, if that's what tickles your fancy. 

Overall, I'd give this game a solid [b]8/10[/b], I enjoyed the time I put into it both in coop and by my lonesome in single player. I'm looking forward to the next entry in the series!

 I believe the producer played Hitman Absolution and was highly inspired by it, or he was the producer of that game and got assigned to this development team; otherwise, what happened to Sniper Elite 5 doesn’t make sense. The game is now highly stealth-oriented. Even the very first tutorial focuses on stealth, and it feels exactly like playing Hitman Absolution. I’m not kidding. So since I played Sniper Elite V2, 3, and 4, this change was not appealing at first. I would even say it was upsetting. But as I got through it and got used to it, I welcomed the change. The fact is you can still go loud. Nazis will call reinforcements but it’s not something one can’t handle. If anything I found it thrilling. Now, since the maps are so much bigger and more complex, additional enemies could feel too much at times. In those situations, I tried to find the alarm first, destroy it, and then start to combat. Scope and boom, scope and boom, just like how I played all the Sniper Elite games.
 You see, however, this game has a way of constantly reminding you that stealth is the proper way to play. It’s not just the tutorial, it’s not just the alarm system either. I think it’s the way the game is designed from the root. So when I played for the second time, I naturally went for stealth and had a completely new experience. It took way much longer, of course, but it was worth it. Searching for ideal positions, spotting and tagging the enemies, finding sound maskers, waiting for sound masking elements like airplanes passing by, deciding whether to use subsonic bullets or not; Oh, it was so much fun! Huhuh 😄. In fact, I would even go far as to say this is the best stealth game I’ve ever played. That being said, the title is totally misleading. This shouldn’t have been Sniper Elite 5. It should’ve been something like “Desert Ghost: France” or something like that, since it’s quite different from other Sniper Elite games.
 Oh, I almost forgot. Submachine guns hit better here. They don’t spread as much. Don’t expect laser accuracy though. 😅
