[u] Sniper Elite 5 is a third person shooter developed and published by Rebellion Developments in 2022. Set during World War II, Sniper Elite 5 is the fifth entry to the Sniper Elite series of video games and features both a full 2 player cooperative campaign. This review will focus on the single player campaign played in cooperative mode. [/u]

[h3] TL;DR – Moving from one strength to another, Sniper Elite 5 is a progressive update of the Sniper Elite series and is easily the best to date with its huge levels and levels of freedom. [/h3]

Story (3/5) – Sniper Elite 5 takes place after the events of Sniper Elite 4 and is chronologically a year before the events of Sniper Elite V2. We are back with the titular sniper, Lieutenant Karl Fairburne, as he works his way through various parts of France and Germany to uncover the mysterious Nazi superweapon, “Operation Kraken”. While the overarching plot is interesting with plenty of lore bits along the way scattered in journals and posters, they merely act as a pre-tense to Sniper Elite 5’s gameplay loop of infiltrate, kill/blow up and exfiltrate. It’s neither overtly memorable nor, offensive in anyway which is perfectly fine. 

Controls (5/5) – Played with mouse and keyboard, Sniper Elite 5 adopts the same control scheme as the previous titles. The default key bindings are logical and easily accessible. Shooting feels natural and the option to adjust sensitivities really help to dial in aiming. Each action/key can be reconfigured to user’s preferences. Moreover, the use of a radial wheel to quickly access the various weapons, ammo types and gadgets make for very intuitive controls of the player’s otherwise very large arsenal.  

Gameplay (4/5) – Just like the games before it, Sniper Elite 5 features a large single map with a main objective and sub-objectives to be completed. How and in what order this is done, is entirely up to the player(s). Everything Sniper Elite 4 does well, 5 does better. Larger maps, more guns, improved traversal and stealth, more verticality, those are just the few improvements Rebellion has made. Stealth and sniping remain to be the core gameplay elements of the Sniper Elite series though, 5 makes it more acceptable than ever to simply go guns a blazing. This level of freedom in such a large playing field makes Sniper Elite 5 such a treat especially when played with a coop buddy. Points are docked for re-playability and some rather questionable enemy AI behaviours. 

Graphics (4/5) – Built on Rebellion’s in-house game engine, Asura, Sniper Elite 5 looks downright gorgeous from its incredibly detailed European castles and cottages to the spanning vistas and artillery shelled trenches. Excellent shadows and lighting also play a key role in bringing these large sets to live especially in the nighttime maps. The core art style and presentation does not differ much from the Sniper Elite series giving it an immediately recognizable feel and look that not many game franchises can claim to have these days. Almost a perfect score if not for the frequent graphical clipping issues encountered when interacting with enemy soldiers. 

Audio (4/5) – From the pop of each silenced gunshot to the boom of a large artillery round landing, the audio experience in Sniper Elite 5 is certainly a treat. Positional audio is serviceable for spotting enemy movements and gun shots. By far the best part is how the myriad of guns in the game have their own audio signature. 

Issues/Optimization – Sniper Elite 5 is very well optimized for the PC and ran well on my system. I had no issues running the game at 4K120 with most of the settings topped out. There were 1-2 hard crashes throughout my playthrough, but nothing serious otherwise. The most common bug you would probably encounter is a graphical one where dead enemies clip through terrain and rag doll in odd ways.

Overall (4/5) – Sniper Elite 5 builds upon all the strengths of Sniper Elite 4 and adds upon it with new gameplay elements that continues to make the game enjoyable. By far the biggest standout for me would be the huge, detailed maps which gives players so much freedom to tackle objectives in however way they see fit. Truly the best in series thus far and a benchmark for a game of this genre. If you can find a cooperative buddy to play this game with, it just makes it that much better. Highly recommended!

Now for tips:

Keep an eye out for Crowbars, Bolt Cutters, and Satchel Charges. They can help achieve objectives, open alternate paths, and open item caches. Crowbars and Bolt Cutters have unlimited uses in the mission where you find them.

When aiming down the sights, enemies with exclamation points over their heads will hear your shot.

Flare guns are rare and can be used to call down artillery bombardments over a small area.

After tagging an enemy with the binoculars, keep your aim on them for another second or two to reveal what they are carrying. This can reveal items like collectibles, intel, and mission items such as keys.

There are optional objectives in missions, but you have to find out what they are. Getting near them on the map, finding intel, or eavesdropping on conversations can unlock them.

Sniper Elite 5: France wastes none of your time in making for a bloody, strategic good time. Every map and mission can be approached in seemingly countless ways; mostly landing on either aggressive, kick-down-the-door style offensive tactics or more by-the-book, stealthy approach to slowly pick apart your enemy from within and afar. It's a f$&!%ing good time!

Gameplay pacing is fairly slow, even if you try rushing things. It truly is intended to be more methodically approached, person-by-person or squad-by-squad. You can push the boundaries a bit but don't expect it to play like a sandbox. It may have very large, open maps that can be approached in many ways - but there are its limits. There are only so many different stealth traps, explosives, or ways to maim your enemy before it starts getting at least slightly repetitive.

While I went in with fairly high expectations, I was still surprised by some of the more standout elements. The level design is top-notch. Take the second mission, this massive chateau with layers upon layers inside. Streets, passages, tunnels—it's like exploring three levels in one. Every replay, I discover something new. And the audio, they've really gone above and beyond. Something I was not expecting at all was after finishing the campaign, you can replay levels with different characters. The kicker— those other characters are ALL fully voiced, responding to what's happening in the game. Adds a whole new layer to the experience. I get the feeling most miss out on even trying this.

While Rebellion didn't stray too far from the mold, something new they did feature is called the Invasion mode. It really spices up the game if you’re willing to take a risk and I wish I had a whole, whole lot sooner. Far too few players ever enable this, not to mention, often wait until very, very late to toggle it on. Basically, if you switch the Invasion option on, as you play the campaign another player can join your game as the enemy sniper. You get more experience by completing objectives while having that option active, but there is always that danger of other players sneaking up on you and messing up your game. It makes you constantly on the edge and looking in all directions while sneaking around. You will usually think twice before sprinting in the open. Anxiety-inducing gameplay has never been so fun! Again though, not enough people seem to utilize this and it will only dwindle further as the game ages out. I do hope they implement this in future releases as it is a lot of fun and holds a lot of potential for more.

I can only imagine what I've missed in the previous entries of the franchise. It seems they regularly go for an 80-93% discount when on sale, so I will likely be picking one or more of those up to check out.

I'd say this is a must-buy for fans of stealth-based combat or for those who enjoy more objective-based, strategic shooters in general. With its still famous kill cam, new weapons, dynamic levels, and that invasion mode—you've got yourself a winner. Until the next sequel, Sniper Elite 5 stands tall as the pinnacle of the franchise.

As a fan of WW2 games and stealth games, I thought this was an amazing game. There are a variety of game modes, such as the campaign, PvP multiplayer, and survival. As an added bonus, if you enjoy hunting achievements like I do, this was a fairly easy game to 100%.

Campaign: I played through the campaign solo on the hardest difficulty as I like to take my time to explore and try to be as stealthy as possible, so I can't say how good the co-op is in this one. I thought the campaign was great, and you'll have even more missions if you get the DLC, and they are worth it in my opinion, especially on sale. The maps are huge, so you can tackle objectives in any order you like, and many objectives have several ways of completing them. Along the way you'll find collectibles and unlock weapons and mobs to customize them. The only real issue I had was the sniping opportunities, as I felt there weren't enough. To get gold medals for snipers, you must get headshots from at least 100m away with them, and I constantly found myself moving around and retreating in certain areas just to achieve that 100m distance. There is a lot of close quarters combat, which I also like, but I think there needs to be more vantage points for sniping.

PvP Multiplayer: I only played one round of this to get the achievement, but I didn't feel the desire to continue playing anymore than that. This isn't really the type of game I'd get for PvP matches. Aside from the base PvP modes, there is also invasion. Invasion allows you to enter someone's game as a German sniper or you can open yours for invading snipers. This adds a good challenge to your game if you find the AI is too easy.

Survival: This is a wave-based game mode where you must survive against 12 waves on enemies. There are a variety of survival missions on a variety of maps. The objective is to hold the command post, and after three waves, you'll unlock the next command post. You do not lose the match if you lose a post, but without them, you won't be able to access their resupply caches. I only played a few rounds of this, but it was quite fun and I recommend this mode if you're a fan of wave-based games.

It pains me not to recommend a Sniper Elite game but this is probably the worst one since Sniper Elite V2. The main problem with V2 was how often they forced you into close quarters combat. This one is ambitious but they ultimately fell short.

The sniping is solid, it's been the same pretty much the whole series. The X-Ray mode is still fun to take a long distance shot, track the bullet, and watch as it kills an enemy, dealing damage to whatever organ you hit. The maps are quite large but the game really forces you to try to sneak instead of snipe.

There are enemies practically everywhere and they hear everything. There aren't many levels with loud noises that can muffle your shots and everything you do is incredibly loud. Enemies hear you moving unless you move at a snail's pace but you can't always move very slowly because you'll get spotted by enemies that can see a long range. The worst part of the sound is there are times enemies shouldn't be able to hear you but still can. For example, there are vehicle patrols in certain maps. If you run 50 feet behind a loud motorcycle, the person on the motorcycle will stop because they hear you. For a game that focuses on ambient sound to muffle your actions, how do you not have that affect a loud motorcycle muffling your footsteps of all things?

The stealth can just be very frustrating and you feel forced to do it. There are certain areas where you can't crawl or you can't crouch and the game doesn't stop you from moving into those areas, it just forces you to stand up. The problem is now you're suddenly running when you expect to be crouch walking and everyone near you hears you, giving away your position. This particularly happened when I had to go under a bridge to disarm bombs. I had to reload my save multiple times because I would step in just the wrong spot, forcing me to stand and alerting all nearby guards. 

Furthermore, there are a lot of areas you think you can vault over but you can't. You'll take your time and the risk of moving through an open area to move towards some cover, with the plan to vault over some sand bags and flank the enemy, to find that you can't vault over these particular sandbags. It happens a lot and there are a lot of these small walls blocking paths you want to take.

​Since there are so many enemies practically everywhere, taking a shot with your sniper rifle will alert most guards and one of them will surely run to an alarm where you'll be left outnumbered and forced to reload your last save. The sniping is fun but you constantly feel punished for doing it and feel forced to move around, silently taking out guards with melee whenever possible.

Sniper Elite 5 is a welcome addition to the Sniper Elite franchise, offering a satisfying stealth experience with its slow-paced gameplay and realistic environments. The game's core mechanics remain unchanged from previous installments, but the new maps and missions provide a refreshing challenge for seasoned players.

The game's stealth mechanics are top-notch, encouraging players to carefully plan their approach and take out enemies silently. The X-ray kill cam remains a highlight, providing a gruesome yet satisfying reward for well-placed shots.

What I particularly enjoyed about Sniper Elite 5 is its relaxing pace. Unlike many action-packed shooters, Sniper Elite 5 allows players to take their time, carefully scouting out enemy positions and planning their next move. This makes for a more immersive and enjoyable experience.

However, the game isn't without its flaws. I initially experienced some motion sickness, but this was easily remedied by lowering the controller sensitivity settings. Additionally, there seems to be a disconnect between the gameplay and the cinematics. My character Karl was wearing a ghillie suit in the game, but he appeared in his default uniform during cutscenes. This created a jarring disconnect and felt like a programming oversight, especially for a game with a premium price tag.

Despite these minor issues, Sniper Elite 5 remains a solid stealth game with plenty to offer fans of the genre. The slow-paced gameplay, realistic environments, and satisfying stealth mechanics make it a worthwhile addition to the series.

It's a step sideways for the franchise and that's not always a terrible thing. And some disclosure here, I got the main game and some DLC on a hefty sale (around 40% off) so perhaps my cost to fun ratio is skewed more in its favor than some other reviewers. I have one big complaint that pops up in other reviews but mostly I'm seeing the same game here.

I'm not going to go do a point for point rehash for my Sniper Elite 4 review, which was pretty solid and a lot of what I said there holds true here. I say that 4 is just more of 3, and in some ways 5 here is just more of the last two.

In 4, I found the open maps to be rather exhausting after a while to the point where on many levels I ended up just going "loud" and whipping out my assault weapon just to speed things up so I could get to some new scenery. My experience with that here in 5 is more of a mixed bag. So far in 9 hours I haven't felt 'bored' by the maps. Enemy patrols are a bit tighter in some places, even clustered, so I spend more time methodically figuring out what I'd consider be a "safe" kill or not, typically considering patrol paths. Don't wanna kill a guy in a gazebo when I know he's got two buddies that wander around the courtyard and might find him. As a result I feel a lot more stealthy and methodical than I did in the previous entry.

My main, big complaint is just the level design.

I find a lot of the design here is a lot more railroad-y than before. The maps have barbed wire, gates, and tunnels that sort of force you down paths and bridges that leave you open to spotters and spawning car patrols. I'll elaborate more on that in a second but I had trouble exfiltrating during the first mission because there was a Y road crossing where I had to go that vehicles kept spawning and piling on top of each other because they'd be constantly "alerted" at my recent dealings there (an exploded car, maybe a body or two) so I had to deal with nearly a full platoon of guys because the game apparently just keeps spawning cars.

So I can't just pick a direction to approach my attack from. Honestly this is fairly realistic, during wartime it makes sense that you'd barb up some hills so any potential stealth teams have a harder time getting to you. I get that but I wish there were more options than "you can only progress through this level by getting past this one bridge". You can have your barbed wire while being a bit more clever with design.

The second level, an estate, is a real crapshow of design. It has the aforementioned three bridges but the real problem is that you're trying to navigate the estate itself. This isn't a problem for say, assassin's creed where most of the game is done with silent stabbings or a bamboo dart tosser. But here, each gun has a "range" of audibility. I have a DLC rifle where its range is pretty short but that 30 or so meters doesn't mean much when I'm trying to snipe at an estate. Once one guy goes down, one of the forty guys gets alerted and it starts a chain reaction that turns my entire minimap yellow and I just had to deal with that for several minutes. I let them wander towards my last known location where I then botch a shot and get forced into open combat, then my minimap is flooded with red because I now have 20 nazis gunning for me. My second run at this level was more successful but I did still have to gun down an entire hallway of six dudes before being able to get out of their sightlines and reset the encounter. I cannot imagine trying to attempt a pure stealth run of that level. There's no way.

That's not the only level where it's like this, either. It's just one of the first ones that made me think "Oh, COME ON."

Previous games had full on sniper nests, typically with a nearby sound masking generator you could kick to start a full sniper spree with, to clear out defensive structures in relative safety as long as you timed your shots right. That's basically gone here. Every now and then your minimap might denote a good spot to snipe from but I've found that generators seem randomly placed and are rarely useful to me. In the estate level there's a generator near the base of one of these towers and when I cleared the camp of enemies I got up and found absolutely no enemies at the edge of the estate to shoot at. So I just cleared the camp and was rewarded with a sound mask and tower with no visible enemies to take advantage of. Come on.

A minor complaint is that you're rewarded with more experience by going for non-lethal takedowns and keeping more Nazis alive or incompacitated. Why... why would I, or anyone, ever want to do that?

I get that this is two paragraphs of good and four of bad but considering the good points of the franchise are still present, it just seems to accentuate what really went wrong with the design. I'm enjoying it though and I'm yearning to play more of it as my Youtube recordings of it are processing in my video editor. Might do some co-op in it. So that's a pretty good sign if a game leaves me with that feeling of "I want to see more".

But yeah the practices around the DLC are pretty bad.

Sniper Elite 5, while boasting a solid core gameplay experience with its strategic sniper mechanics and detailed environments, faces notable challenges stemming from its community issues. Here’s a constructive critique focusing on these aspects:

1. Community Feedback Integration: There appears to be a disconnect between player feedback and in-game improvements. Many players feel that their concerns, such as balance issues or bugs, are not being adequately addressed. A more responsive approach to community feedback, including regular updates and clear communication, could help build trust and improve player satisfaction.

2. Host Kicking Issues: Host kicking—where a player who hosts a match can eject others—also poses a problem. While the feature is designed to give hosts control over their matches, it can be abused to kick players who perform well or to manipulate match outcomes unfairly. This can lead to an uneven playing experience and frustrate players who are simply looking to enjoy a competitive game.

3. Vote Kicking Abuse: In Sniper Elite 5, the vote kicking system is intended to help players manage disruptive behavior. However, this system is frequently misused. Players often exploit it to remove opponents who are perceived as skilled or as threats, rather than dealing with genuine disruptive behavior. This misuse not only hampers fair play but also discourages players from engaging with the game’s competitive modes, as they may find themselves unfairly targeted and removed.

Sniper Elite 5 suffers from significant community issues, primarily characterized by abuse of vote kicking and host kicking features. These problems lead to unfair removals of players, often based on personal grudges rather than actual disruptive behavior. This misuse of in-game systems creates a toxic environment, undermining the game’s competitive integrity and making the multiplayer experience less enjoyable for many players. Addressing these issues through improved moderation and refined game mechanics could help mitigate these problems and foster a more positive community.

Alright, listen up, folks! This game, right, it's like the lovechild of Sniper Elite 4 and a bunch of new cool features. Rebellion didn't mess with the winning recipe; they just sprinkled in some extra spice. You know that saying, "If it ain't broke, don't fix it"? Well, Rebellion got the memo, and in the world of modern gaming, that's like finding a vegan at a barbecue – unexpected and refreshing.

The gameplay is tighter than my jeans after Thanksgiving dinner. Movement, weapons – it's like they've been on a CrossFit regimen. The AI got a facelift, too, but let's be real, it's a stealth game, not a Mensa meeting. Invasion Mode? That's the cherry on top – it's like playing hide and seek, but with bullets. And who doesn't love non-lethal options? I mean, sparing Nazis for XP is a bit like getting a participation trophy for world-saving, but hey, options are options.

The story? Yeah, it's there, like a background hum. Think John Wick – you're not here for Shakespeare; you're here for headshots. The multiplayer? It's a party!

Killcams? They've upgraded from a boring organ slideshow to a full-blown action movie. Bullet holes, blood spats – it's like Tarantino joined the dev team. Sure, I have a few gripes – like, why no destruction physics on character models? I want to blow a guy's jaw off and see the aftermath, not a pristine chin!

In a nutshell, this game might be the franchise's MVP. It's a must for Sniper Elite veterans, shooter enthusiasts, and stealth nerds. Go ahead, grab it – maybe throw in the DLC for good measure. It's like a gaming buffet, and you're the VIP guest.

Alright. It's fun. As in, really ridiculously fun. There's a lot of little changes from Sniper Elite 4 that give #5 a breath of fresh air. And I'm glad I came to this game a little late as well, because a lot of the bugginess other people are reporting seems to have been fixed. Not completely, but it's definitely playable.

If you don't know what the Sniper Elite series is about, it's basically a WW2 sneaky-shooty-snipey type of deal with a lot of depth in its combat and stealth mechanics. The usual suspects like noise and sight, concealment and light and dark. Objects in the environment and map can provide sound-masking, to cover up the noise of your weapon, such as an artillery piece firing, planes firing overhead, generators you sabotage, and so on.

The AI is something praiseworthy. The average schmuck stands about and follows a set patrol route, as you'd expect. Alert them, though, and that's where the AI shows its depth. Enemies will take cover and triangulate your position from missed shots or watching their buddies get killed. The average soldier is indecisive and slow. Commanded by officers, they begin to exhibit more intelligence, spreading out and circling around you. In later levels, the elite soldiers that appear more frequently are absolutely vicious, pushing up using cover and suppressive fire, flanking you in the blink of an eye, and grenading anything they can't see. It really tests your understanding of the AI and your ability to use your surroundings.

Nothing particularly big has changed since #4. Most of the changes I'd say are quality-of-life and immersion improvements. Weapon customization is one of the best new features, letting you spec out every rifle / secondary / pistol for specific tasks, and it's good. Really good. Non-DLC weapons have all their customization options unlocked through side objectives rather than grinding out a challenge. The sound system is now more nuanced and some places have ambient noise that masks sprinting. It's much rarer for collectibles to be on random soldiers so there's less rifling through every single dead body that #4 was annoying about. You can't swap out your weapons except at a workbench but you can pick up every dropped enemy weapon as a temporary 4th weapon and with a perk take its ammo, so ammo is generally more plentiful. Oh yeah, and iron sights. I've been playing largely with iron sights on every weapon that allows them because it's so much fun and so immersive.

More so than in #4 as well, there's usually multiple ways to accomplish an objective. Stealth is usually more viable than going in guns blazing, but you could do the latter, if you're good at repositioning and snap shots.

Where Sniper Elite 5 really shines is in co-op. Having a buddy alongside you makes games infinitely more fun. Now you can plan out sequences to take out groups of guards, have two separate loadouts tailored to different engagement types, and flank the flankers. It's an incredible, incredible joy to play.

Edit:
Another thing I want to mention is the difficulty. There is a whole range of difficulty options that vastly change how the game is played, to the point where it can feel like an entirely different game. On its easiest setting, it's possible to mow down waves of enemies with a machine-gun, shoot out tanks with armor-piercing pistol rounds, and snipe enemies all the way across the map casually. On Authentic, the game turns into an absolutely brutal cat-and-mouse affair, with you being the hunted just as often as not. It's exhilarating in all the best ways.

I've only bought the base game and downloaded the free DLCs, and I'd say I easily got my money's worth. I can't speak to the paid DLCs, though I'll probably get them only when they're on sale.

"Let me start by saying that Karl Fairburne is one of the coolest characters in video games. He doesn't use cringe-worthy or awkward dialogue that makes me cringe and drop the game. He's pretty cool, and I also like his attire. So, the main character gets a solid 9/10 from me.

I appreciate that there isn't a lengthy and complicated tutorial in the game. Instead, you have a short and straightforward tutorial before diving into the game. I give this aspect an 8/10 because overly complex and long tutorials can make a first-person shooter boring. However, I had a slight issue with not knowing how to heal initially. It might have been my mistake for missing it, but it would be helpful if the game explained which button to press for healing.

The variety of guns in the game is fantastic, and I like that the game explains their historical usage in a simple and concise manner. It's impressive, and I've learned about guns I never knew were used. The fact that guns can make different noises depending on their loudness adds depth to gameplay. So, this aspect gets a perfect 10/10.

I admire that Sniper Elite 5 includes elements that many other AAA games wouldn't dare to touch, unlike titles like Call of Duty. The game provides an authentic World War II experience, and even using terms like 'Nazi' and featuring the Nazi flag was surprising to me, as many games have avoided them since 2005. I appreciate that the game uses accurate terms like 'Fritz,' 'Heinies,' or 'Kraut.' It feels more genuine than generic labels like 'bad guys' or 'evil people.' This aspect deserves a 10/10 for its boldness and respect for historical accuracy.

Thank you for giving German voice actors a chance. It makes the characters feel genuinely German, unlike Ubisoft, who didn't use Swedish actors for Assassin's Creed Valhalla. This approach often results in incorrect pronunciations and disconnects from the culture. Kudos to Sniper Elite 5 for giving voice actors from the respective countries a chance, and I appreciate that effort. It makes me happy to see this attention to detail.

I also love how the soldiers' dialogue feels like it's meant for them, making the game feel more real and immersive. It's a subtle but important touch that adds to the overall experience.

Moreover, when you press 'B' to use your binoculars for scouting, and you can see their names and some personal information, it adds a layer of complexity to the game. Sometimes, it can make you feel conflicted about taking a shot, depending on what you've learned about them. It adds an emotional dimension to the gameplay that can be both engaging and thought-provoking.

Regarding bugs or lag, I purchased the game a bit late, so I can't comment on its early state. However, I didn't encounter any major bugs, just some minor issues like soldiers occasionally bunny hopping or having creepy, open mouths. So, I'd rate it 8/10 for the relatively smooth experience.

I like the game's map and how it creates an immersive environment that isn't empty. It's great that you can find items scattered around. However, I did notice that some areas are inexplicably blocked, which was a bit confusing. So, I'd give this aspect a 7/10.

The menu design is good; gray and blue colors work well, and it's simple and visually appealing. While it's not a big deal, it could be interesting to see different menu designs for various locations in the game. So, the menu gets an 8/10.

Overall, Sniper Elite 5 offers a solid gaming experience with a few minor quirks, making it an enjoyable addition to the series. Ladies and gentlemen, gather 'round as we dive headfirst into the mesmerizing black hole of pointlessness that is Sniper Elite 5. If you've ever wondered what it would be like to play a game that defies every expectation, where boredom is the main attraction, then congratulations, you've stumbled upon gaming's magnum opus of nihilistic irony.

Sniper Elite 5's brilliance lies in its ability to take everything you've come to expect from a game and turn it on its head. The game opens with all the enthusiasm of a sloth in a sedative-induced coma, introducing you to Karl Fairburne, the protagonist who probably questions the meaning of life more than you do. His mission? Well, it doesn't really matter, because nothing in this game does.

The gameplay is a masterpiece of absurdity. It revolves around the concept of hiding behind cover, waiting for enemies who seem just as clueless about their existence as you are about yours, and then engaging in a slow-motion ballet of monotony as you line up your shots. Each kill is punctuated by an X-ray kill cam, which serves as a stark reminder of the sheer absurdity of it all. It's as if the game is saying, "Look at this! Isn't it ridiculous?"

The AI, or lack thereof, is a work of art in itself. Enemies saunter around like they're on a leisurely stroll through a warzone, and they hardly react when their comrades mysteriously drop dead around them. It's almost as if they've given up on life, just like you while playing this game.

As for the story, it's a narrative rollercoaster that somehow manages to go in a straight line. Characters deliver their lines with all the enthusiasm of someone reading the phone book. You'll find yourself chuckling at the sheer absurdity of trying to care about a plot that seems more interested in mocking you than engaging you.

Graphically, Sniper Elite 5 pushes the boundaries of mediocrity. The environments are as exciting as watching paint dry, which, ironically, might actually be more engaging. Character models look like they were rendered by a bored intern, and the animations are so stiff that you'll wonder if everyone in this game is secretly made of cardboard.

Sound design is another exercise in ironic indifference. The soundtrack seems to be on a never-ending loop of monotony, while the voice acting delivers lines with all the emotion of a malfunctioning robot. It's as if the game is laughing at you for even bothering to listen.

In conclusion, Sniper Elite 5 is a nihilistic and ironic masterpiece of tedium. It revels in its own absurdity, inviting you to join in on the joke. If you're in the mood for a game that not only embraces boredom but turns it into an art form, then Sniper Elite 5 is your ticket to a hilariously pointless gaming experience. Just remember, in the grand scheme of things, nothing really matters, and neither does this game. Enjoy! Or don't. It doesn't matter, anyway.

Sniper Elite 5 doesn't just raise the bar; it sets a new standard for tactical shooters. Rebellion Developments has crafted a masterpiece that combines precision gameplay with a riveting narrative, delivering an immersive experience that keeps you on the edge of your seat.

From the first bullet fired, Sniper Elite 5 demonstrates a level of realism that's both awe-inspiring and challenging. The attention to detail in the game mechanics is nothing short of exceptional. Every shot feels deliberate, and every decision matters. Whether you're choosing the perfect vantage point or managing your resources, the game rewards strategic thinking and patience.

The level design is a testament to the developer's dedication to creating a dynamic, living world. Each environment feels meticulously crafted, offering a range of strategic options for players. Whether you're perched atop a crumbling building, navigating a dense forest, or infiltrating an enemy stronghold, the game invites you to explore and adapt.

The addition of new tools and gadgets adds depth to the gameplay, providing players with creative ways to approach each mission. From suppressed weapons for stealthy takedowns to environmental traps that turn the tide in your favor, Sniper Elite 5 empowers players with an arsenal that complements the methodical nature of sniping.

The narrative is both engaging and emotionally resonant, weaving a story of espionage and intrigue against the backdrop of World War II. The characters are well-developed, and their interactions add a human touch to the high-stakes missions. The campaign's pacing keeps you invested, with each mission offering a fresh set of challenges and objectives.

The game's signature slow-motion kill cam returns, and it's as satisfying as ever. Watching a perfectly executed shot in glorious detail never gets old. It not only serves as a testament to your skill but also adds a cinematic flair to the overall experience.

Multiplayer modes, including cooperative play and competitive matches, enhance the replayability of Sniper Elite 5. The thrill of outsmarting opponents or coordinating with teammates adds another layer to an already compelling package.

In conclusion, Sniper Elite 5 stands tall as a triumph in the genre. It's a game that demands precision, rewards strategy, and captivates with its immersive world. Whether you're a fan of stealth, tactical shooters, or gripping narratives, Sniper Elite 5 hits the bullseye and then some. It's not just a game; it's a testament to the art of sniping. Lock and load, sharpshooters – this one's a must-play.

+ Great way to scratch a WW2 shooter itch.
+ A good looking game that's well optimised. Consistently runs at high FPS and doesn't seem to jerk or stutter at all.
+ Accommodates different play styles. Sniper only, run-and-gun, stealth/non-lethal.
+ Huge maps with different routes and several objectives. If you're planning a non-lethal/stealth run, prepare to spend several hours per map.
+ Granular difficulty controls, can easily fine tune to your specific tastes.
+ Unique multiplayer modes. Axis Invasions are the highlight; another player can enter your PvE mission and try to hunt you down, or you can do the same to someone else. Short queue times if you're invading. There's also a dedicated sniper mode called "No Cross"; essentially, two teams snipe at each other across the map.
- The story... exists. You're John Elite, you're running around France sabotaging Nazi plans. That's it.
- Cheeky to suggest there are nine maps when number nine is essentially a thirty second epilogue. In reality, there are eight (plus DLC) full fat campaign maps.
- AI a bit weird at times. Even with the increased aggressiveness setting, they sometimes don't seem too concerned about investigating dead bodies or trying to co-ordinate flanks. Other times, if spotted, you'll be shot at with laser accuracy across large distances by pistols and SMGs. Tanks like to camp and stare at you incessantly.
- Enemy footsteps don't seem to exist in this universe.
- Maps aren't completely open. There are some routes and paths that are deliberately blocked.
- Axis Invasions seem to happen at the worst possible time (at least for me), when a mistake has been made or there's already pressure from the AI. When I've invaded other games, it tends to be on earlier maps in the campaign, possibly with other players still figuring out the game.
- The several other multiplayer modes are dead. There were about seven or eight custom games at the time of writing, five of which were Rebellion servers with zero players. I didn't go in expecting a vibrant multiplayer community, but it's something to keep in mind.

Sniper Elite 5 - First Impression Review

I'm writing this as a Sniper Elite 4 vet, and you should read this if you have already played SE4. If you haven't, feel free to read it also.

The question is, "Should I spend my time on Sniper Elite 5?". The answer is Yes, if you're familiar with the Sniper Elite franchise.

Graphically wise, it's improved from the last game(which is Sniper Elite 4, by the way). The color is much more defined, although it didn't overshadow the last game. Texture wise, things such as rocks and foliages and buildings, are not much different from SE4, unless you're counting pixels. Water looks better, although not significantly. Ballistic looks more enjoyable. Kill cam is more intimate and more casual. Body movements have been improved: Karl now ascending/ descending stairs with careful steps rather than running/ stampeding through as seen in SE4. Sniper Rifle's Scopes has more natural sway to it. Soldiers can be spotted wearing watches, added more realism to it.
Conclusion, it's improved, the same way GOW Ragnarok compared to GOW. 

Gameplay is more or less the same. I would say that this game adopted several key mechanisms from The Last of Us. Infinite stones for distraction are now replaced with limited bottles. Infinite Satchel Charges from SE4 are now replaced with Satchel Charges picked up from battlefields(you can still carry an inhuman amount of them, however). SE5 now introduced work benches(again, The Last of Us), with significantly more weapon adjustments compared to SE3(rudimentary) or SE4(non-existent). 
You might have seen some reviews online saying that SE5 is not as big as SE4, which is debatable. I would say that the maps are more compact but still big. It still can stump an SE4 vet like me from time to time. 
Picking up weapons from battlefields is no longer something you can do freely as in SE4, but I like it as it's significantly realistic. You can't just pick up a Sniper Rifle from the field and fire it, it doesn't work like that. However, you're allowed to use it as Temporary, which is acceptable. There are many more varieties to pick up from the field as well: weapons with attachments that give you advantages. 
Weapon Wheel is the same.
God vision, or something called Enemy Position has also been replaced with zones of interest(a colored circle that signifies the whereabouts of an enemy). Why, hello there, Ghost Recon Wildlands, I have missed you. This makes it more important to tag enemies, as you're no longer given the Detective Vision back in SE4.
Iron Sight is now officially in the game. Love it.
You can now take out enemies with non-lethal melee technique as well. Guess that they're slowing down after all the gruesome close-combat takedowns back in SE4. 
There are also fewer enemies in SE5, compared to SE4. In SE4, thanks to God vision, you can take out an entire base of enemies, like 20 or 30 of them Nazis, but here in SE5, even 3 to 4 of them is already some struggle. I personally think it's more intimate.

Music is not a thing. The warrior of Rome motif in SE4 is no longer here. I don't miss it particularly, but this is also a different game anyway. I would say that the Alarm sounds remind me of Wolfenstein a lot. It's okay, i don't think people are too hung up on the music department for this game.

The game ran well on my dated machine! It heated up the machine even less than SE4, what a relief!. Kudos to you, Rebellion.

As of now, the complete edition is quite expensive, but i'm happy with my Deluxe Edition. Will be purchasing the full Edition in the future.

The game is good, i will greenlit it if you ask me. That's all I have to say for now.

To be honest, I am kinda torn. I love this game, even though it's really uneven - it does some things better than its predecessor (weapon customization for instance is a tad better than challenges-upgrades from 4th installment), while some it does worse (optimalization is rather below average). 

Worst offender is a price - I bought it on a sale, but still, managed to buy only one season pass with the vanilla game and it still cost me around 25$, pretty steep I daresay. I don't care for storyline, cause it was always mediocre at best in the series. GFX-wise, it's just a SE4 with some tweaks here and there - and by "tweaks" I can also mean "some textures don't load properly at times", though it's nothing gamebraking. What IS gamebraking, are bugs - sometimes enemies dissapear after a takedown, sometimes you can't take a proper aim at something with your scope, at times game can CTD or get laggy for a few seconds out of the blue. Also, to nitpick a bit - skill tree is even worse than SE4. Could be gone completely and nobody would even notice. Animations are a tad better, but still on the bad side. AI is more stupid than my boss. 

So yeah, to keep it simple and sum it up - game should have at least a half year more development time, but can still give you lots of fun. If you like killing nazis, it's for you. 

tl;dr - expensive and with bugs, but still worth it on sale and if you like killing nazis

Sure you can mod weapons now, which I really like; but only 6 sniper rifles in the base game is extremely stingy & greedy.  Rifles like the Mosin Nagant that you'd expect to be in the base game are now locked behind a paid DLC wall. Things just haven't massively evolved enough since SE3 (visually or otherwise) for them to continue asking these kind of outrageous prices.  This might be arguably the best game in the franchise, though many fans would disagree (myself included), & say that that title belongs to 4. I like how you're instantly transported to the new control point during survival as opposed to having to make a mad dash to the new point and try to hurriedly set up every 3 waves. I like the variety of the campaign maps and how different each is visually to the others, and I do enjoy how survival mode has different operations that people can choose to do - it freshens things up, even if the changes in the bases are only a few meters away. I like knocking people out, putting their bodies in a pile, and then blowing them up; it's the only use I've got for the non-lethal ammo, bottles, and sneak incaps. I also like being able to temporarily pick up fallen enemy weapons and use them, but am disappointed that I can't permanently switch to them if I wanted to. It was an option in SE4, as opposed to only having them for a single clip's worth of ammo and Karl throwing the gun away afterward.

Additionally, while I do appreciate the dev team for doing something new and taking the game in a slightly different direction than SE4 so it doesn't feel like they're trying to sell you the same game again, I can't help but feel that they also took out a bit of what made SE fun. 

I miss chaining Teller mines, S-mines, and trip mines together in a long line, torturing the tank operators by running around their disabled rig and pelting it with TNT, and blowing it all sky-high with a flare gun finale as explosions rip through the map.

Vehicles no longer explode quite as nicely when compared to the previous iteration. While they're understandably tankier and more resistant to explosives (it takes over 11 TNTs to blow up a tank as compared to 2-4 TNTs in SE4), it sometimes feels like a chore to get rid of them in survival. This is also true when considering that satchels are now counted as items and not a limitless thing Karl magically pulls out of his underwear instantly to kill a tank/armored car whenever a prompt appears (placing and detonating a satchel in SE5 no longer means the vehicle is insta-killed, only crippled). I also miss being able to blow up the patrol boats with a 1-2 well-placed shots. 

There aren't a lot of nice places to snipe >100 meters within the base game, so you're better off grinding mission #9 for the rifle medals/masteries. It's also the only mission where you can speedrun and finish in less than 5 seconds. It's kind of anti-climatic, as opposed to the last mission in SE4 when you take down a man and his plane.

Actually, the game is pretty bereft in terms of places where you can snipe when considering it as a whole.

Sure, you get vantage points, but the maps are weirdly super busy (many buildings or obstructions), or empty (nothing but barren fields) in places. In both cases, there's only a few soldiers milling about, and trying to snipe with your rifle (as opposed to walking up to them and waving hello with your pistol or SMG) is unsatisfying. There's a noticeable lack of enemies as opposed to in SE4, giving the impression that it's relatively unoccupied, even when you're in a supposedly highly guarded top secret facility. The difference is noticeable when you directly pit random SE4 and SE5 maps against each other.

There's exceptionally few spots where you can snipe more than a few people at a time. One of the only few spots that comes to mind is the chateau/mansion balcony opposite of the tea house in the Wolf Mountain DLC. This is diametrically opposed to SE4, in which there's plenty of vantage points to mow people down with your trusty rifle. Compare SE4's Regilino Viaduct or Magazzeno Facility to SE5's War Factory or Secret Weapons. ...Especially the Regilino Viaduct map to the Secret Weapons map. You have an absolutely wonderful long-shot view the moment you're spawned in the default starting location in both of them, but there's only 1 soldier to snipe from that view in SW as opposed to the ~dozen or so in RV.

As mentioned above, I am disappointed that ripping people's calves open and blowing their legs off with a single mine isn't as visually exciting. The S-mine and trip mine have been replaced by the Schu mine, which, while versatile, tends to have a smaller explosion radius. It most likely will only tear apart 1 person instead of a few in a single blow. I see it as more of a sabotage weapon than a defensive trap, especially during survival.

I do like incapping enemies, nailing the buddies that try to rescue them, and watching them bleed out. The noble tradition of tea-bagging is optional. It's fun. 

Some mechanics are occasionally bugged. Some kills sometimes aren't counted as ghost kills, despite the enemy being completely unaware of Karl's presence, the soldier being the only enemy around in 50 meters, and is not being observed by others at the time of death.

Mixed feelings about this episode. Let's get the monetization right out of the way: it's absolutely ridiculous and nobody should ever buy this Complete Edition or any of the Season Passes (if you already own the base game) full price, just wait till next Black Friday sales to see prices collapse by -50% and then buy what you're missing, or just watch for keys on Instant Gaming. The asking price for the amount and quality of content you get is disproportionate and pushes the string way too hard, there's much to rethink here when making Sniper Elite 6.

About content now... On the positive side: 
- some maps are absolutely amazing (Spy Academy, Kraken Awakes, Landing Force, Secret Weapons) in both gameplay & design
- Invasion mode is extremely fun on both sides and really adds a neat & fresh feature without penalizing the invaded player (because even if you're killed you just reload the latest checkpoint and you're good to go)
- Modding is mostly ok despite the fact that you can create ludicrous weapons that should never exist, but oh well, whatever at this point I guess?
- Being able to shoot SMGs and pistols in first person is a much welcome novelty (shouldn't be in any shooter game in 2023, but it seems like Sniper Elite still has a way to go on many features that have been considered as standard for years now).

On the negative side? Well, sadly - pretty much everything else:
- Most maps feel desperately empty of enemies.
- Too hard of a focus has been put in this episode on SMG gunplay instead of rifle gunplay, which is ironic considering the game's very title: many maps have mostly been designed around CQC combat instead of sniping. Most sniping spots feature a very limited number of accessible targets, or feel like a missed opportunity altogether like Conqueror's castle tower, which features such a thick wall that your firing angles are ridiculously limited. Also, natural progression on many maps is an uphill one instead of a downhill one, which is weird and counterproductive for a would-be professional sniper who needs high ground to find vantage points...
- Authentic difficulty is a joke compared to previous games and only removes the red diamond on the scope when aiming, yet it's still very easy to hit enemies at whatever distance using the very convenient white dashes to draw virtual lines. A long-requested-never-delivered Authentic Plus experience for the most hardcore players should be a thing, but obviously won't be anymore.
- Enemy AI is mostly terrible, but above all wonky and unpredictable. On some maps (for instance Kraken Awakes), the enemies will track you down and represent a real threat, which is awesome; on others (for instance Landing Force), they will just hide or run to random locations instead of actively trying to locate the threat and coordinate an assault... Overall, the AI is too passive and would deserve becoming much more agressive and cunning.
- Compared to Sniper Elite 3 & 4, Sniper Elite 5's arsenal is extremely limited, featuring only 1/4th of the rifles available in previous episodes. One of the original developper claims was that they wanted to make more unique guns and thus preferred quality over quantity, but this claim fell flat notably thanks to the modding system which allows you to mod very different guns to feel very similar, so the outcome was just a much poorer choice of instruments of death. Also, Trip Mines never made it back to this game for absolutely no reason despite player requests from Day 1. What we got instead were totally useless Shumines that only stun enemies (and not even special units). Why??
- Too much of a focus was put into night maps instead of day maps.
- Many gamebreaking bugs haven't been fixed yet (you can't vault over certain obstacles that are the exact same size or even lower than others that you can vault; some barriers and ledges don't allow you to shoot on targets below despite Karl playing his peeking-out animation; the climbing and descending stairs animation is ridiculous and stiff; looting animation is way too long and can get you killed; putting interacting with corpses and melee on the same key was insanely stupid and often results in you starting to loot a corpse while actually trying to ambush an enemy, especially if it's an invading player Jaeger; some scripted snipers appear out of nowhere and instantly shoot you down without warning, which can lead to an instant Game Over on Authentic difficulty... and the list can go on).
- Subjectively speaking, customization is pretty poor for both Karl & weapons. Karl's OK but could have been extended; weapon camos are straight up atrocious and don't belong to this game.
- Survival mode isn't fun in solo and often forces you to defend weird positions not suitable for any kind of defense. Wrong balancing I guess, or just an artificial way of creating difficulty where there shouldn't be any.
- Lastly, the scenario is bland at best, but truth be told, Sniper Elite has never shined for its storytelling so I guess that's fine.

On a side note, can't comment on Multiplayer because I just don't care a second about competitive gameplay, especially in this kind of games.

All in all, Sniper Elite 4 is still to this day the best Sniper Elite episode in the series: ALL maps are sniper-friendly; the weapon arsenal to choose from is massive; the setting - Italy - features awesome landscapes bathed in bright daylight; all DLC missions are amazing in terms of setting, content and size... 
Sniper Elite 5 seems to have forgotten the roots of the series, aka being a SNIPER game, and neither the map design nor the arsenal encourage you to play as a sniper (one of the most blatant examples being Festung Guernsey where you have a HUGE point of view on 80% of the map... where the (very few) targets present mostly hide underground ^^). On top of that, very few maps really stand out, the others being either generic or forgettable, or almost copy-pasted from Sniper Elite 4 (hello Rough Landing) but in a poor manner.
Is it sheer incompetence? Or a brand new, inexperienced developper team that took over the franchise and had to relearn from 0 the basics of the series, not undertanding the game's DNA and thus making in the process all the mistakes that were progressively learnt between Sniper Elite 1 and Sniper Elite 4...? Whatever be the answer, one can only hope Sniper Elite 6 will be an episode a la Sniper Elite 4 expanded with the good features from Sniper Elite 5 (player invasions, FPS gunplay, fluent map traversal). And a much more adequate pricing for the content offered.

My final verdict after 244 hours is: 
- if you have already played Sniper Elite 4, 3 and 2 and are starving for more, then yes, get Sniper Elite 5 AT A DISCOUNT. Never pay the full price asked for this game, it does NOT deserve it.
- if you have never played a Sniper Elite game, then definitely skip this one and buy Sniper Elite 4 instead, you'll have an amazing time and lots of content to handle for only a handful of eurodollars (the game is dirt cheap these days). Grab Sniper Elite 5 at a huge discount only AFTER you finished Sniper Elite 4, but be aware that you'll only get a fraction of the content of Sniper Elite 4 in this game.

Despite SE5 not being a TERRIBLE game by any stretch (as my hours played counter indicates), my recommendation vote however is based on the uproar against the full asking price for this product, which is hilariously disproportionate, as well as a much missed opportunity to make a much better game than this one ended up being, especially considering the setting chosen - occupied France, which could and should have been the soil for so many cool stories to tell and places to visit and the fact I'm French myself.

[h1]A Masterpiece Unveiled - Sniper Elite 5 Review[/h1]

[b]As an ardent fan of the Sniper Elite series, I've been captivated by its immersive gameplay and meticulous attention to historical detail from the very beginning. With the release of Sniper Elite 5, my admiration for this franchise has reached new heights. Set against the backdrop of war-torn France in 1944, this latest installment continues to follow the journey of the iconic Karl Fairburne as he battles the enigmatic "Project Kraken."

From the moment I stepped into the virtual world of Sniper Elite 5, I was greeted by breathtaking vistas and meticulously crafted environments. The landscapes are a testament to the developer's commitment to recreating the atmosphere of wartime France. Each mission is a marvel in itself, with sprawling maps that invite exploration and a level of detail that leaves no corner unexplored.

One of the most striking features of Sniper Elite 5 is the painstakingly recreated architecture of the era. Every street, building, and structure feels authentic, transporting players back in time to the tumultuous 1940s. The commitment to historical accuracy enhances the immersion and makes every encounter within the game world feel incredibly genuine.

What truly sets Sniper Elite 5 apart is the sheer diversity and scale of each mission. Every mission is a work of art, intricately designed to be visually stunning, unique, and endlessly engaging. The addition of new gameplay mechanics, such as the ability to hide in high grass, scale walls and pipes, and conceal fallen enemies, has completely transformed the strategic landscape. These innovations demand players to adapt and strategize like never before, leading to an entirely fresh experience.

The introduction of "starting positions" is a brilliant stroke that empowers players to unlock new vantage points as they progress through missions. This not only enriches replayability but also allows for a dynamic evolution of playstyle and strategy. These starting positions have become an invaluable tool for mastering missions, ultimately enhancing the overall enjoyment of the game.

The arsenal of weaponry and accessories at players' disposal is truly remarkable. The inclusion of different types of ammunition adds an extra layer of tactical depth, influencing decision-making and encouraging players to explore new strategies. The hallmark feature of the series, the X-ray kill cam, has been refined to perfection in Sniper Elite 5. The bone-crushing realism of every shot, whether from a rifle, pistol, or machine gun, is astonishing. The level of detail in the depiction of bodily organs during these sequences is both shocking and awe-inspiring.

Visually, Sniper Elite 5 is a marvel, with stunning locations and landscapes that push the boundaries of what modern gaming can achieve. The game's graphics are a testament to the developer's dedication to creating a visually immersive experience that does justice to the era it portrays.

Furthermore, the extensive range of post-launch DLC missions is a testament to the developer's commitment to keeping players engaged and entertained long after the game's initial release. This consistent support has added considerable value to the game and ensured that fans like me remain enthralled.

The multiplayer experience in Sniper Elite 5 is a well-crafted affair, with a robust anti-cheat system that has virtually eliminated the scourge of cheaters. This has rejuvenated the multiplayer community and breathed new life into the competitive aspect of the game.

In closing, it's clear that words alone can't encompass the entirety of Sniper Elite 5's brilliance. This game is a testament to Rebellion's dedication to excellence, and as a devoted fan, I am immensely grateful for the opportunity to traverse the battlefields of wartime France with Karl Fairburne once again. Sniper Elite 5 is not just a game; it's an experience that has left an indelible mark on my gaming journey. Kudos to Rebellion for crafting a masterpiece that has brought immeasurable joy to fans like me.[/b]

I played and beat the crap out of this game on PS5, and loved it. It some getting used to, and the story was absolutely terrible and forgettable. The main character is annoying af, constantly talking to himself in gruff McMilitary man voice... But, the gameplay, and the levels, are fascinating. Playing a campaign with an online friend, is great. Having that same campaign be invaded by an enemy player adds tension where there never used to be. I'm shocked not many games have this invading feature. It makes the game so much more unpredictable, and fun! You lose nothing by dying; just restart. And the you can rematch or close invasions as many times as you want. I can't tell you how satisfying it is to play this game online.

However, there are some mechanics that are extremely dumb. The A.I. (like with all stealth games) throw themselves into your line of fire, and don't act intelligently. Like with every stealth game since MGS3, enemies hear footsteps, and immediately turn around to think its an enemies, regardless of the fact that they're surrounded by hundreds of other soldiers who are constantly walking around them. 

When you lie prone to snipe, your whole body moves, instead of the camera, to look around. This gives your position very easily to enemies, while prone.

There seems to be no camouflage system in place with different outfits. I could be laying in grass in a field in my Ghillie suit, any enemy from a distance will start to have their detection meter go up, despite not moving. Taking out lights, and hiding in shade, also doesn't seem to affect this detection meter. 

Overall, Sniper Elite 5 has some problems, but I keep coming back to it for the fun as hell level design, co-op experience, and invasion mechanic. To me, they make the game extremely replayable, even after finishing the rather short main campaign. The only other thing that really isn't acceptable is the price of their DLC and Season Passes, but that's up to you decide if it's worth it. Companies will always keep doing these things, so enjoy what was, for how long it is.

Above all I have had great fun, and it continues to be fun.  Isn't that what games should be?

CON - THIS NEEDS FIXED YESTERDAY AND UNBELIEVABLE IT STILL ISN'T, ESPECIALLY WITH THE AMOUNT OF COMPLAINTS ALL OVER FORUMS:

I like the game, but, significant caveats and/or warnings:

#1 - This isn't about sniping much of the time. Thus far, most kills are probably under 100m, and a large number are even under 50m. Scoped rifles almost seem like a liability in some missions... the first mission, rounding corners constantly and going through narrow bunkers, I used a Thompson and a MG-42 most of the mission. Soooo.... more like SMG-Elite 5, especially compared to the previous game, SE 4, where a number of missions did have larger open areas to snipe from.

#2 - I read reviews about invisible walls, but that's not really it. The problem is the clipping is wildly chaotic. Sometimes, I can walk right up to a hedge... other times, I'm colliding with it despite the graphics showing another 6-8 feet of space before I should be touching it at all. This makes sniping over hedges and low walls a pain. Not so much an issue of navigation (mini-map tells you basically what can be moved across), but more an issue of sloppy clipping design around some areas of terrain.

#3 - Invasions aren't my thing. Played with them off the whole time so far, so one of the major changes of the game I am not even really experiencing. I don't want to play MP, so, that's a change that is lost on me I guess.

#4 - Movement feels worse than SE 4. I'm either running too fast, walking to slow, or crouch-walking about right. Karl will just freak out at full speed trying to find the angle to open a door sometimes, so hitting the Z key to walk or Ctrl to crouch is how I slow down when I need to, but it's too slow for advancing forward all that far. Speed of movement is a little off.


Overall, though, it's a fun game if you approach it as a combo of Wolfenstein and Hitman. It feels a lot like another universe where Wolfenstein is less dark and Hitman is less stealthy. I really enjoy blasting away with the SMGs and throwing grenades and using traps... but I'm not sure that's what players were expecting, especially since SE 4 had much more open maps. SE 5 still has those sniping mechanics, but after a fun little practice with the 1,000 meter target in the training area, I've since been making most shots, often with SMGs, at a distance under 100m, which is a bit odd. But that's how the map design pushes the player to play. Even the DLC maps sometimes feel not that open, with buildings and corners to clear more often than large open horizons.

Again, really fun, but not that much sniping despite the name.

This isn't the game you think it is. It's not bad, but it's not a game about being a sniper.
There are precious few sniping spots in the missions, and very few objectives that demand usage of your sniper skills. The levels are quite constrained compared to the previous game, and there's a LOT of space that isn't traversable or usable.
Player movement is worse than previous games - the environment is much more visually 'noisy' now, and mantle/jump is less consistent. There are often knee-high obstacles you can't step over, but can't mantle either. There are also lots and lots of places where you can't jump/hang, but it seems like you should be able to. The cover system is improved, but still prone to nasty bouts of stickiness at the worst possible times.
I can't speak to the invasion system - maybe it's the secret sauce that makes this a 9/10 - but I can't see how it improves the base gameplay. There's already very little sniping, having another player trying to hunt you down is only going to make it more tedious to peel the onion on these levels.
The upgrade system, previously only tied to objectives, is now ALSO tied to finding hidden objects in levels, which makes it even more likely that you'll go through most of the game without seeing a lot of the content than previous games.
The 'special target' system is good - giving specific kill requirements adds the thimbleful of extra thought to their deaths that makes it more than just another speedbump in the missions.
The 'targets of opportunity' that show up as optional objectives are nice, but I found only one mission where it wasn't guaranteed that you'd be given those objectives through normal play.
Adding multiple spawn points to each mission is a wierd extra system to spend time on - there's basically no variation in how the missions play out, I'm not sure why Rebellion thought anyone would want to play them more than once. If you've gotten all the objectives, you've seen everything the mission has to offer.

In conclusion - This feels like Rebellion wanted to make a Hitman game with asymmetric multiplayer. It's not that, it's about 30-40% of that, and in the process they lost most of what made Sniper Elite 4 a good game. I'd have gladly paid 60$ for "Sniper Elite 4: 10 more missions edition," but this isn't even close.

It's... fine for 10$, but it clearly cost way too much to make to sell it for 10$.

[h1]IF YOU ARE LOOKING AT THIS GAME WITHOUT EXPERIENCE WITH THE SERIES:[/h1]


[i]Sniper Elite[/i] is best described as an open-level stealth series, but that's simplifying it a bit. You're dropped into an extremely large open level as a WW2 allied powers commando, with a set of gear you've decided on before the mission consisting of a rifle, a secondary weapon (Usually an SMG or shotgun), and a sidearm. This, plus some usable items, will be your backbone as you work your way through a set of pre-defined objectives all across each level's map. The backbone of your arsenal is your rifle, SE puts massive emphasis on an accurate sniping experience with simulated bullet drop, range adjusting, wind offset, bullet penetration, ricochet, etc. Your difficulty selection will decide how many of these interfering factors are enabled, and how many assist tools are provided to deal with them. All difficulties below the extreme range allow the "steady your aim" function to also gradually reveal exactly where your bullet will land, letting players still getting used to the mechanics score consistent shots at the cost of needing to invest more time to land a sure hit. 


This emphasis on your rifle also ties into stealth. The level's ambient noise as well as nearby loud props can help mask the sound of your fire, and since enemies will be hunting you over long distances their AI is designed to try and narrow down your location and flank around it, boxing you in and basing their strategy off of where they last were alerted to your presence. This unique formula of stealth over often incredibly large distances also means that going loud is perfectly viable since even unsuppressed shots can only be heard so far and the WW2 setting means separate groups of pursuing soldiers can struggle to communicate with each other. It's helpful to think of Sniper Elite as a sort of Commando Simulator, rather than pure stealth as optimal gameplay as in Metal Gear or Splinter Cell. To further this levels are scattered with items and weapons for you to stock up or swap your loadout with, and secondary objectives such as documents or optional side-quests to fulfill for higher completion. 


Because of the open-ended level design and nature of stealth games campaign missions are generally meant to be replayed to perfection, and progress is tracked with an XP system that rewards passive upgrades to your character and gear. Sniping itself is a skill you'll become more comfortable with too as you play, with time I found I was learning to predict shots well enough even without the assist features, and this massively opens up how you can interact with levels. - The weapons customization looks fun initially, but I'm not a big fan of it. I fear this took a lot of development time, Time that could have been spend into other more important things. What I do love it the fact you could choose your scope. That's the only customization I truly love, appreciate & want to see in SE6. 
- The wind mechanics in SE4 were better then in SE5. 
- The personal skills you unlock for Karl in the single player, there are some skills in there that you didn't have before in earlier games. These skills make the game way easier & I don't really understand why you receive these skills.

- Mission 8, oh boi I suffered, that one was a though cookie to crack. This 1 might be the only one that strongly recommends you to be stealthy and remain stealthy. 
- All other missions were top knotch, exactly what you would expect. Multiple entry points, multiple ways to get somewhere, secret passages, alarm posts you could deactivate, explosion barrels here and there. 
- The implementation of finding satchels, crowbar and bolt cutters is a good move. It really drives you to look around for stuff like intel & ammo, not just enemies. 
- The cutscenes you get are not wanted, not necessary, the developers shouldn't have wasted their precious & expensive development time on creating strong women just because it's a F hot woke topic these days. Stick to your core gameplay and just offer us a good mission intel before and after the mission. Strong women are so saturated these days that I personally nearly gag each time it gets shoved into my visual cortex. That US ranger that was present in earlier games, could have been the only buddy with boots on the ground you need. Since you have been in this war together for a rather 'long' time, but no he was just another a$$hol€ He had zero added value, you could have cutted him out aswell at this point. No camaderie, no brother in arms, no band of brothers, nothing, just another prick whining about rules. & Karl... apparently prefers to listen to a random wahmen, instead of actually listening & talking to this US ranger that has been assisting Karl the whole campaign in previous installments with solid mission intel.

I just finished playing through Sniper Elite 5, and let me tell you, it's an absolute blast! Now, I know there were some reviews floating around claiming that this version wasn't true to its sniping roots, but trust me, they couldn't be more wrong. This game is all about sniping, stealth, and it's seriously awesome. If you've been playing it like a run-and-gun shooter, then you've been missing out on the real deal. So, buckle up and let me break it down for you.

First things first, Sniper Elite 5 nails the sniper experience. The developers have gone all out to make it feel authentic and intense. The visuals are stunning, and the attention to detail is insane. Whether you're stalking through a heavily guarded enemy base or perched on a crumbling building overlooking a war-torn city, you'll be blown away by the realistic environments and the sheer scope of the maps. Trust me, it's like stepping into a World War II movie.

But let's talk about the gameplay, because that's where Sniper Elite 5 truly shines. It's all about being patient and methodical. You have to study the enemy's movements, factor in wind and bullet drop, and time your shots perfectly. And let me tell you, when you line up that perfect shot and see the slow-motion X-ray kill cams, it's like nothing else. You'll witness bone-crushing impacts and organs getting shredded by your bullets. It's so satisfying, and it adds a whole new level of realism to the game.

Now, sniping is the main focus, but that doesn't mean you can't get your stealth on. Sniper Elite 5 has a solid stealth system that lets you silently take down high-value targets and infiltrate enemy territory undetected. You'll have access to cool gadgets like silenced pistols and throwable distractions, giving you plenty of options to play it your way. The level design is fantastic too, encouraging exploration and rewarding strategic planning.

Now, let's talk replayability. Sniper Elite 5 has got you covered. Each mission offers multiple paths and optional objectives, so you can go back and try different approaches. And if you're up for some co-op action, the game has multiplayer modes where you can team up with a buddy and tackle missions together.

But, I'll be real with you. Sniper Elite 5 isn't without a few minor flaws. The enemy AI can be a bit wonky at times, doing some weird stuff that breaks the immersion. And there might be the occasional performance hiccup or graphical glitch, but nothing major that ruins the overall experience.

So, if you're into sniping, intense action, and methodical gameplay, Sniper Elite 5 is a game you don't want to miss. Don't let those misleading reviews steer you wrong. Grab your sniper rifle, dive into this immersive World War II adventure, and prepare for some heart-pounding moments. This game is the real deal, and I highly recommend it. Happy sniping, everyone!

EDIT 7/26/2023:  After taking a break from trying to play this game and then doing some digging, it turns out this game has at least 2 issues going on at the same time:
1.  has trouble running in DX12, you most likely will start getting "device lost" errors and the game will start freezing up at random times, even causing game to lock up to point where you'll have to use task manager to stop game, so run the game in VULKAN api
2.  all ULTRA settings are borked, they cause VRAM leakage which eventually cause game to freeze/laggy/hitching due to running out of VRAM.  does't matter if you have highest end card with 24GB of vram, seen some reviews of those with 3090TI having this problem.  I have a 4070 running game at 1440p, looks awesome at ultra, but then the above happens after a little while. turn down settings to high and problem is immediately gone!

I honestly don't see much, if any difference in ULTRA to HIGH, it sucks this game has issues and I still don't recommend getting it.  but if you do go ahead and buy it anyway, keep in mind the above and  it should help

I am a fan of this series and I have played parts of SE2 and 3, all of SE4.

Now SE5 is a big let down.

The developers always have some weird tastes when it comes to a sniper game. In SE3, they wanted us to sniper tanks...countless tanks. In SE5, they want us to do CQB.

Just look at the screenshots on the store page. Half of them are CQB or non-sniping fights. Why do I need to do those? This is Sniper Elite, not just some WW2 Agent game.

SE4 was nearly perfect. Everything was better than SE5.

Things that SE4 had done right but failed in SE5:
1. Level design. SE4 was a sniper game. SE5 is a game where you play a guy who kills an entire city of Nazis without having to be quiet.
2. Again level design. SE4 was way less linear.
3. Customization. SE5 DOES NOT allow stealth play until you are late into the campaign to unlock muzzles. SE4 had stealth rifles (with severely reduced damage, which tested the player's skills) from the start.
4. SE4's Karl's movement was way less clunky.
5. SE5 is INSANELY big. It seems that it downloads all the DLCs even if you don't buy them. It took 100G on my disk.

Other than some graphical glitches here and there, which are pretty minor. This game is fantastic, the Rebellion team overhauled the gameplay. Still plays and feels like the previous games, but instead of being stuck on a linear trail or focus in levels, you now have a much bigger play area, to explore, and use multiple avenues to complete tasks. Not to mention, multiple objectives to be completed, whether its the main mission, an assassination target, or gathering intel/supplies or taking out outposts and other locations within the map. Highly recommended for fans of the franchise
